Reflective of this, the assessment, identification and management of PROMs are frequently overlooked in routine clinical care. Moreover, the instruments used to evaluate PROMS are inconsistent and heterogenous [ ]. In attempt to standardise this, the PMR-impact scale (PMR-IS) was proposed as a PMR-specific PROM composite score [ ]. The PMR-IS comprises four subdomains including symptoms, physical functioning, emotional and psychological wellbeing and finally GC-related side effects [ ]. Upon external validation, all subdomains demonstrated good measurement properties, with the exception of the GC-related side effect subdomain which failed to demonstrate adequate internal consistency and construct validity [ ]. Consequently, the PMR-IS will require further validation prior to its incorporation into routine clinical practice, and indeed future clinical trials and studies. Regarding GC-related side effects, the novel STEROID-PRO has demonstrated validity and reliability for measuring the impact of GC therapy from the patient perspective in a large multinational cohort with multiple rheumatic diseases, including PMR [ ]. Using four subscales including social impact, impact on appearance, psychological impact and treatment concerns, the 15-item STEROID PRO aims to accurately measure and capture the impact of GCs across rheumatic diseases [ ]. Ongoing validation of the STEROID-PRO will be critical to ensuring its reliability, sensitivity to change and utility both in research studies and routine clinical care of those with PMR. Recently, it was reported that one in four patients with PMR are affected by depression [ ]. In that study, depression was strongly associated with poor physical function, underscoring the psychological impact of physical limitations in PMR, and highlighting the importance of identifying and managing comorbid depression in this population [ ]. Additionally, another recent publication by the same Australian group demonstrated the persistence of fatigue at 18 months post diagnosis of PMR, with over one-third of patients also reporting a perceived failure to recover to a premorbid physical function despite almost 2 years of standard care [ ]. This not only has a potential significant negative impact on disease activity and treatment response but also HRQOL [ ]. Moreover, the persistence of fatigue and perceived failure to recover to a premorbid physical function raise concerns over the effectiveness of our current treatment paradigm to adequately treat those with PMR, and underscores the urgent need for a new holistic and comprehensive approach to PMR management, including both pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions. This was further emphasised in the PROMs data from the SAPHYR trial, which highlighted how the general health and physical functioning of those with relapsing PMR is grossly impaired across multiple domains, and fails to improve by week 52 for those on GC monotherapy [ ]. To the contrary, treatment with the IL-6 inhibitor sarilumab accompanied by a 14-week GC taper achieved robust and clinically meaningful improvements in HRQOL and PROMs [ ]. It is evident, therefore, that by embracing new management approaches there is potential to modify the patient experience, and subsequently overall disease outcomes. Non-pharmacological Management Patient education is paramount to achieving optimal outcomes in PMR, as it supports self-management and fosters shared decision-making. The T2T recommendations suggest that all patients with PMR, and their caregivers, should receive information pertaining to PMR clinical disease features, treatment-related benefits and adverse effects, comorbidities and potential complications [ ]. In order to ensure adherence to therapy, all patients need to be educated on the role of GCs and the importance of compliance with their individualised prescribed GC taper. Given the overlap of PMR with GCA, all patients should be educated on GCA, its symptoms and risks, and advised to seek immediate medical attention should they develop any characteristic symptoms [ ]. Whilst the primary source of education should be the primary medical physician, patient charities are also a valuable information resource [ ]. The evidence on the role of non-pharmacological therapies including nutrition, physical activity and complementary therapies in PMR management is scarce. Despite this, the 2015 EULAR/ACR PMR management guidelines do recommend “considering an individualised exercise programme for PMR patients aimed at the maintenance of muscle mass and function, and reducing risk of falls” [ ]. Despite this recommendation, in the PMR cohort study, only 17% of those with PMR reported using exercise to manage their PMR, and only one-quarter of patients received specific exercise advice from their treating physician [ ]. In order to improve the awareness and educate patients, and indeed healthcare professionals appropriately on the role of exercise in PMR, we need to strengthen the evidence base with adequately powered, well-designed trials of specific exercise interventions and their impact on long-term outcomes in PMR. In the interim, although there is no direct evidence on the optimal type or duration of physical activity

]. Despite this recommendation, in the PMR cohort study, only 17% of those with PMR reported using exercise to manage their PMR, and only one-quarter of patients received specific exercise advice from their treating physician [ ]. In order to improve the awareness and educate patients, and indeed healthcare professionals appropriately on the role of exercise in PMR, we need to strengthen the evidence base with adequately powered, well-designed trials of specific exercise interventions and their impact on long-term outcomes in PMR. In the interim, although there is no direct evidence on the optimal type or duration of physical activity for those with PMR, the benefits of physical activity in general, including improved functional independence, maintenance of muscle mass and function, reduced falls risk, preservation of bone mineral density, promotion of weight loss, enhanced cardiovascular health, and improvements in PROMs such as fatigue and depression, are likely to positively impact overall outcomes in this population [ – ]. Therefore, physical activity should be actively advocated for and promoted by all healthcare professionals. Moreover, the role of the full multidisciplinary team, in particular physiotherapists, should be optimised to provide safe, effective and individualised exercise programs. Patients with PMR tend to be chronologically older, and show signs of accelerated aging with a higher prevalence of geriatric syndromes including sarcopenia and frailty [ ]. The ubiquitous use of GCs and their impact on muscle mass is likely contributory. This presents unique challenges that underscore the importance of a holistic approach to PMR care, with multidisciplinary care and geriatric principles at the helm [ ]. Additionally, addressing the burden of polypharmacy in this older, comorbid population and implementing “deprescribing” to improve medication use where appropriate is essential to reduce adverse effects, drug–drug interactions and drug–disease interactions [ ]. Finally, the use of GC and other immunosuppressive agents in this older patient cohort is associated with a higher risk of infection. Therefore, it is imperative that all patients are educated on the importance of vaccinations, in particular influenza, pneumococcal and herpes zoster vaccines, to ensure their timely administration and reduce associated morbidity [ ]. Therapeutic Agents in PMR Glucocorticoids GCs have been the mainstay of PMR treatment for decades. Whilst there is no evidence-based, standardised protocol for steroid taper, the 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendation suggests starting with a prednisone dose equivalent (PDE) between 12.5 and 25 mg per day [ ]. The specific dose chosen within this range is primarily physician-led and patient-specific, tailored to comorbidities, likelihood of GC-related adverse events and risk of relapse. Characteristically, patients experience a profound and rapid resolution in their symptomatology upon introduction of GCs. Once remission is achieved, GCs should be tapered gradually; however, the optimal tapering strategy remains controversial largely because of the paucity of studies addressing it [ ]. Previously, isolated PMR was considered a relatively “mild” condition, with most patients anticipated to complete their GC course within a 12-month period. However, we now recognise that for a significant majority of patients, their disease course is marked by frequent relapses and subsequent huge GC burdens over a number of years [ , , ]. Indeed, a meta-analysis of observational studies reported the pooled proportions of individuals still using GCs at 1, 2, and 5 years were 77% (95% CI 71–83%), 51% (95% CI 41–61%), and 25% (95% CI 15–36%), respectively [ ]. Data from the ACR Rheumatology Informatics System for Effectiveness (RISE) registry reported 63.8% of those with PMR remained on GCs at 12–24 months, of whom only 39% were prescribed a GC-sparing agent [ ]. This long-term use of GCs is suboptimal, and highlights the significant shortcomings in our current management paradigm of isolated PMR. Moreover, those with PMR are typically older, frailer [ ] and so more vulnerable to the well-recognised adverse effects of GC therapy. Up to 85% of patients with PMR experience at least one GC-associated adverse effect [ , ]. This substantial GC-related toxicity coupled with the high relapse rate underscores the urgent need for effective GC-sparing therapies. Despite this, currently no pharmacotherapeutics apart from GCs are recommended as stand-alone first-line treatments in isolated PMR. Management of GC-Related Adverse Events The well-recognised GC-related adverse events frame a significant proportion of the treatment experience of those with PMR [ – ]. Nearly 70 different GC-associated toxicities affecting the musculoskeletal, dermatologic, ocular, endocrine, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, neuropsychiatric and immunologic systems have been described [ – ]. It is important to monitor for such GC-related toxicity and identify those who may require closer monitoring. The Glucocorticoid Toxicity Index (GTI) is a standardised composite instrument developed by an international group of physician-investigators from several medical subspecialties, aiming to measure change in GC-related toxicity across two time points [ ]. It has undergone validation in both real-world clinical studies and clinical trials [ ]. Although its ease of use

of those with PMR [ – ]. Nearly 70 different GC-associated toxicities affecting the musculoskeletal, dermatologic, ocular, endocrine, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, neuropsychiatric and immunologic systems have been described [ – ]. It is important to monitor for such GC-related toxicity and identify those who may require closer monitoring. The Glucocorticoid Toxicity Index (GTI) is a standardised composite instrument developed by an international group of physician-investigators from several medical subspecialties, aiming to measure change in GC-related toxicity across two time points [ ]. It has undergone validation in both real-world clinical studies and clinical trials [ ]. Although its ease of use has been demonstrated, it has yet to be integrated into routine clinical care to guide management decisions. The EULAR recommendations for monitoring adverse events of low dose GC therapy were published in 2010 [ ]. Despite the significant GC-associated toxicities identified, the monitoring strategies proposed are vague, in stark contrast to those of GC-sparing agents, such as methotrexate, which have well-characterised and rigid monitoring protocols [ ]. Musculoskeletal effects include GC-induced myopathy and reduced bone mineral density (BMD) with osteoporosis and fragility fractures. GC-related myopathy typically affects the proximal skeletal muscles and is characterised by pain-free weakness and muscle atrophy which affects physical performance. It can be difficult to differentiate clinically from symptoms of PMR and its many disease mimics. EULAR recommends that GC-related muscle weakness should be assessed “through questioning” at the start and end of treatment in clinical trials [ ]. We advocate that in addition to enquiring about typical steroid myopathy symptoms (difficulty climbing stairs, raising from a chair or lifting objects) at each clinic visit, patient education on the importance of exercise initiatives be emphasised, with proactive early referral to physiotherapy as appropriate. BMD decreases even with low dose GCs and there is an increased risk of osteoporosis and fractures with higher GC doses and cumulative GC burden [ , ]. There is substantial morbidity and associated healthcare costs associated with fractures, particularly in older adults. It is important to note, however, that although GCs contribute significantly to reduced BMD, the aetiopathogenesis of osteoporosis is typically multifactorial in PMR and indeed other inflammatory rheumatic diseases [ ]. Systemic inflammation associated with poorly controlled disease activity, low physical activity, poor nutrition, older age and hormonal loss secondary to menopause all negatively impact bone health [ ]. Therefore, optimisation of these factors and a multimodal approach to osteoporosis management is essential. The ACR guidelines for the prevention and treatment of GC-induced osteoporosis recommend that all adults ≥ 40 years of age, which is representative of all patients with PMR, should have their fracture risk estimated using the fracture risk assessment tool (FRAX), and undergo BMD testing within 6 months of the initial GC treatment [ ]. Every 12 months, fracture risk should be reassessed, and BMD retesting should be performed every 1–3 years if not on osteoporosis prophylaxis, or every 2–3 years if established on osteoporosis prophylaxis therapy, outside of calcium and vitamin D [ ]. All patients should have their calcium (1–1.2 g/day) and vitamin D (target serum level ≥ 20 ng/ml) intake optimised [ ]. All patients with PMR (women ≥ 40 years old, and men ≥ 40 years who are at moderate to high risk of fracture) should be treated with an oral bisphosphonate [ ]. Where an oral bisphosphonate is not suitable an intravenous bisphosphonate should be considered, and failing this, dependent on local restrictions and reimbursement policies, teriparatide should be considered. If none of these are appropriate, denosumab (a monoclonal antibody inhibitor of RANK ligand) should be commenced [ ]. Endocrine and metabolic adverse effects of GCs include hyperglycaemia, insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, weight gain, adrenal suppression, cushingoid features and growth suppression [ – ]. EULAR recommends that all patients should undergo fasting blood glucose levels and trough oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) at the start and end of therapy [ ]. The BSR guidelines on the other hand recommend 3-monthly glucose testing [ ]. If a patient has pre-existing diabetes, prior to the commencement of GC, they require very careful monitoring, and early consideration of a GC-sparing agent [ ]. Cardiovascular adverse effects include arterial hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and heart failure [ – , ]. EULAR and BSR recommend screening for hypertension and other cardiovascular risk factors prior to the commencement of GCs [ , ]. Patients should also be regularly assessed for GC-associated neuropsychiatric effects ranging from minor mood changes, mood swings, irritability, depression and anxiety to mania, psychosis and cognitive impairment and dementia [ ]. The predominant gastrointestinal effect of GC is gastric irritation and ulceration, for which EULAR recommend routine monitoring (e.g. checking haemoglobin levels) and prophylactic gastroprotective treatment (e.g. proton pump inhibitors) where necessary [ ]. The most common ocular complications of GCs are cataract

heart failure [ – , ]. EULAR and BSR recommend screening for hypertension and other cardiovascular risk factors prior to the commencement of GCs [ , ]. Patients should also be regularly assessed for GC-associated neuropsychiatric effects ranging from minor mood changes, mood swings, irritability, depression and anxiety to mania, psychosis and cognitive impairment and dementia [ ]. The predominant gastrointestinal effect of GC is gastric irritation and ulceration, for which EULAR recommend routine monitoring (e.g. checking haemoglobin levels) and prophylactic gastroprotective treatment (e.g. proton pump inhibitors) where necessary [ ]. The most common ocular complications of GCs are cataract formation and glaucoma. EULAR recommends baseline ophthalmologic evaluation for both in all patients commencing high dose GCs [ ]. Given the failure of current guidelines to comprehensively provide guidance for accurate and regular monitoring of well-recognised GC-associated side effects, we outline our proposed monitoring and prophylactic therapeutic strategy for GC-related adverse events in those with PMR in Fig. . Whilst our proposed strategy is comprehensive, each PMR patient should be individually considered, as there may be marked heterogeneity in overall cumulative GC burden between individual patients, and a variable vulnerability to the occurrence and severity of related side effects. Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs Conventional Synthetic Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs The efficacy of conventional synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) in isolated PMR remains uncertain, with studies yielding inconsistent findings. The most studied, and indeed used csDMARD, is methotrexate (MTX) [ ]. Its clinical efficacy in the management of PMR has been reported in three RCTs, albeit with mixed results [ – ]. Two of the studies demonstrated the efficacy of MTX [ , ], whereas the third failed to show any GC-sparing benefit [ ]. The studies supporting the efficacy of MTXs were of higher methodological quality; however, the total number of patients investigated in the RCTs is low ( n = 194). Notably, only low dosages of MTX, equivalent to or less than 10 mg, were evaluated in these trial populations, and one may therefore postulate that a higher dosage would yield alternative findings. The results of a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, “PMR MODE” (NL8366), assessing the efficacy of MTX at a dose of 25 mg per week in addition to a 24-week prednisolone taper are highly anticipated to answer this question [ ]. Moreover, the “STERLING-PMR” (ISRCTN17828080) trial examining the role of MTX and leflunomide (LEF) in patients with PMR who have experienced at least one disease relapse is currently ongoing. It is a phase 3 open-labelled RCT comparing standard care plus MTX (starting dose of 15 mg, progressively increased to 25 mg, or reduced to 10 mg if not tolerated) or LEF if MTX is not effective or not tolerated. Despite the conflicting results and lack of clear evidence showing any true reduction in GC-related adverse events, the 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations include a conditional recommendation to consider the early incorporation of MTX with a GC regimen in those at increased risk of GC-related adverse events or prolonged disease course [ ]. Moreover, these recommendations also recommend MTX in those experiencing relapse with an inadequate response to GC or GC-related adverse events on follow-up [ ]. The recent French Society of Rheumatology guidelines for the management of PMR also recommend MTX as an alternative to IL-6 inhibitors in GC-dependent PMR [ ]. Until recently, the role of LEF as a GC-sparing agent in refractory PMR was supported only by two case series [ , ]. However, a multicentre observational study by Vinicki et al. compared the use of MTX ( n = 143; median dose 15 mg/week) and LEF ( n = 43; 20 mg/day fixed dose) as GC-sparing agents, and reported the superiority of LEF for achieving remission and GC discontinuation ( p = 0.001) [ ]. Furthermore, the time until GC discontinuation was shorter in the LEF group (median 4.7 months) versus the MTX group (median 31.8 months) ( p < 0.001) [ ]. Although this fosters promise for the use of LEF in refractory PMR, several important limitations must be considered. These include its non-randomised design, the lack of a specified GC starting dose or tapering regimen (which was left to the treating physicians discretion), and the higher CRP and ESR levels in the MTX group at baseline and at the time of enrolment suggesting potentially greater disease activity. Additionally, a large number of patients in the MTX group received doses of 15 mg or less, which may represent underdosing and could have contributed to its apparent inferiority [ ]. Therefore, the results of the ongoing randomised, double blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial “PMRLEFRCT” ( NCT03576794 ), which is assessing daily leflunomide 20 mg in combination with a 26-week GC tapering regimen, are highly anticipated to clarify the role of LEF in the management algorithm of PMR. Additionally, a large number of patients in the MTX group received doses of 15 mg or less, which may represent underdosing and could have contributed to its apparent inferiority [ ]. Therefore, the results of the ongoing randomised, double blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial “PMRLEFRCT” ( NCT03576794 ), which is assessing daily leflunomide 20 mg in combination with a 26-week GC tapering regimen, are highly anticipated to clarify the role of LEF in the management algorithm of PMR. Additionally, the results of STERLING-PMR (ISRCTN17828080), as described above, will provide valuable insight into the role of LEF in the management of PMR. Azathioprine is another csDMARD whose role in PMR has been evaluated in an RCT [ ]. Although the investigators reported a significantly lower mean prednisolone dose at 52 weeks in the azathioprine group (1.9 mg) compared to placebo (4.2 mg), its use was associated with a higher incidence of adverse events [ ]. Moreover, the study was limited by a small sample size and a high dropout rate [ ]. Biologic Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs Interleukin-6 Antagonists Given the pivotal role of interleukin-6 (IL-6) in the pathogenesis of PMR, and the consistently elevated levels of serum IL-6 levels in those with active disease [ ], the exploration of the efficacy of IL-6 antagonists in PMR has ushered in a new era in the management of PMR. Following the positive results of the pivotal SAPHYR study ( NCT03600818 ), sarilumab, a fully human anti-IL-6 receptor alpha monoclonal antibody, was approved for the management of refractory PMR by the FDA in 2023 [ ]. This phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT evaluated the efficacy and safety of subcutaneously administered sarilumab in 118 patients with active GC-refractory PMR on 7.5 mg/day prednisolone [ ]. A significantly higher number of patients in the sarilumab group (200 mg every 2 weeks, with 14-week GC taper) compared with the comparator group (placebo every 2 weeks with 52-week GC taper) achieved sustained remission from weeks 12 to 52 (28.3% vs. 10.3%; p = 0.0193) [ ]. Additionally, at week 52, the cumulative GC burden was significantly lower in the sarilumab (777 mg) vs. placebo group (2044 mg) ( p < 0.001), with the GTI also favouring the sarilumab group [97 (76–121.5)] compared with the placebo group [112.5 (85–141)] [ ]. The most commonly reported adverse event during sarilumab treatment was neutropenia, which occurred in 15% of patients and resulted in treatment discontinuation in 12% [ ]. Notably, no infections were associated with the neutropenia. However, white blood cell counts should be carefully monitored in those treated with sarilumab, with dose adjustment or cessation of therapy as appropriate, should neutropenia occur. Tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antagonist, has also had positive outcomes in two phase 3 trials [ , ]. The SEMAPHORE study ( NCT02908217 ), a phase 3, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled RCT, examined the efficacy of intravenously administered tocilizumab in those with GC-dependent PMR, requiring doses of prednisolone ≥ 10 mg per day [ ]. A total of 101 patients were randomly assigned to receive tocilizumab at a dose of 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks or placebo every 4 weeks, with both groups undergoing a predefined standardised tapering of orally administered prednisolone [ ]. The primary outcome of a CRP-PMR-AS < 10, in addition to attainment of a prednisolone dose of 5 mg per day or a reduction in prednisolone dose by 10 mg from baseline at week 24, was achieved in 67.3% of those in the tocilizumab group compared to 31.4% in the placebo group ( p < 0.001) [ ]; 49% of patients in the tocilizumab arm were no longer receiving GCs at 24 weeks compared to 19.6% in the placebo arm ( p < 0.001) [ ]. The PMR SPARE ( NCT03263715 ) double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase 2/3 RCT evaluated the use of tocilizumab in 36 newly diagnosed, treatment-naïve patients with PMR [ ]. Those in the tocilizumab group received 162 mg subcutaneously every week along with an 11-week GC taper, whilst the placebo group received a weekly placebo, in addition to the same 11-week GC taper [ ]. At 16 weeks, GC-free remission was achieved in 12 out of 19 patients (63.2%) receiving tocilizumab compared with 2 out of 17 patients (11.8%) receiving placebo ( p = 0.002) [ ]. The median cumulative GC burden was also less in the tocilizumab arm (727 mg) compared to the placebo arm (935 mg) ( p = 0.003) [ ]. Despite the positive results from both these studies, with each one meeting their primary endpoint (Table ), and despite the successful indication of tocilizumab in patients with GCA, it has to date failed to attain regulatory approval

The median cumulative GC burden was also less in the tocilizumab arm (727 mg) compared to the placebo arm (935 mg) ( p = 0.003) [ ]. Despite the positive results from both these studies, with each one meeting their primary endpoint (Table ), and despite the successful indication of tocilizumab in patients with GCA, it has to date failed to attain regulatory approval for use in patients with isolated PMR. Moreover, whilst the regulatory approval of sarilumab represents a pivotal step in the advancement of PMR care, several unanswered questions remain, including the role of sarilumab in newly diagnosed patients, and the optimal therapeutic duration and method of treatment withdrawal. Additionally, given the effects of IL-6 inhibitors on the acute phase reactants CRP and ESR, there is an urgent need for a reliable serum biomarker to assess disease activity. Investigational Targeted Therapies Anti-Tumour Necrosis Factor Alpha Agents Early observational studies suggested potential efficacy of tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) antagonists in PMR [ , ]. However, two subsequent phase 3 RCTs failed to confirm a meaningful therapeutic effect (Table ) [ , ]. The largest of these RCTs investigated infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal anti-TNFα antibody, in 51 newly diagnosed, GC-naïve patients with PMR [ ]. Participants were randomised to receive either intravenously administered infliximab (3 mg/kg) or placebo, in combination with a 16-week GC taper [ ]. At 52 weeks, there was no significant difference in the primary endpoint (proportion of patients relapse free) between groups [ ]. Secondary outcomes, including the number and duration of relapses, in addition to cumulative GC exposure were also comparable [ ]. A smaller phase 3 RCT evaluated etanercept, a recombinant human TNF dimeric receptor fusion protein, at a dose of 25 mg subcutaneously biweekly or placebo, in 20 newly diagnosed patients with PMR [ ]. Patients did not receive any GCs in either group, and after 14 days, the PMR-AS score decreased by 24% from baseline ( p = 0.01) in the etanercept group; however, the score remained unchanged in the placebo group ( p > 0.05) [ ]. Given the modest improvement only with etanercept, and the failure of infliximab to meet its primary endpoint, no further studies are currently planned to examine TNFα antagonists in PMR. Nonetheless, important limitations should be acknowledged. Both RCTs were small in scale and the etanercept trial had an exceptionally short follow-up of only 14 days [ ]. Moreover, both studies evaluated the use of anti-TNFα agents in new-onset PMR, and as such, their use in established refractory PMR remains unknown, and may warrant further investigation. B Cell Inhibition Growing evidence suggests a potential role for B cells in the pathophysiology of PMR, given the presence of an altered peripheral B cell distribution in active disease [ , ]. This is also supported by the findings of the BRIDGE-PMR RCT and its 1-year extension study, which demonstrated that B cell depletion with rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, may be effective in treating PMR (Table ) [ ]. This proof-of-concept 21-week RCT demonstrated the benefit of a single 1-g dose of rituximab, in addition to a 17-week prednisolone taper, in achieving GC-free remission at 21 weeks (48% in rituximab group versus 21% in the placebo group; p = 0.049) in both newly diagnosed patients and those with refractory PMR [ ]. In the 1-year extension study, 47% of those in the rituximab group versus 23% in the placebo group ( p = 0.12) remained in GC-free remission at 52 weeks following the initial single 1-g dose of rituximab [ ]. There are currently two further RCTs with longer follow-up periods underway: the REDUCE-PMR-1 ( NCT05533125 ) evaluating rituximab in new-onset PMR, and REDUCE-PMR-2 ( NCT05533164 ) evaluating rituximab in relapsing PMR. CTLA4 Fusion Protein Abatacept is a fusion protein of the extracellular domain of the human cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) which is linked to a modified Fc of human immunoglobulin 1 (IgG1) that modulates the T cell co-stimulatory signal. Given the involvement of T cells in the pathogenesis of PMR [ , ], abatacept underwent evaluation in those with early-onset PMR in a phase 3, multicentre, double-blinded placebo-controlled RCT, the ALORS study (Table ) [ ]. Patients were randomised to receive either abatacept (18 patients) or placebo subcutaneously in combination with a 12-week GC taper (16 patients). Fifty percent in the abatacept group versus 22% in the placebo group reached the primary endpoint at week 12 which was the obtainment of a CRP-PMR-AS ≤ 10, without GC or rescue treatment; however, the difference did not reach statistical significance

Given the involvement of T cells in the pathogenesis of PMR [ , ], abatacept underwent evaluation in those with early-onset PMR in a phase 3, multicentre, double-blinded placebo-controlled RCT, the ALORS study (Table ) [ ]. Patients were randomised to receive either abatacept (18 patients) or placebo subcutaneously in combination with a 12-week GC taper (16 patients). Fifty percent in the abatacept group versus 22% in the placebo group reached the primary endpoint at week 12 which was the obtainment of a CRP-PMR-AS ≤ 10, without GC or rescue treatment; however, the difference did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.07) [ ]. Upon further analysis, no significant differences were observed in cumulative GC dose between the two groups at week 12 and 36 [ ]. Moreover, the effect of abatacept on CRP-PMR-AS was predominantly driven by reduction in CRP, with minimal impact on pain, physician global assessment or other PROMS [ ]. Consequently, no other trials evaluating abatacept are underway or planned. Janus Kinase Inhibitors The Janus kinase (JAK) family of intracellular tyrosine kinases, which comprises JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and tyrosine kinase (TYK) 2, in association with signal transducers and activators of transcription (STAT) have a pivotal role in mediating the downstream signalling of a significant number of proinflammatory cytokines. Subsequently, the role of the JAK/STAT pathway and its targeted inhibition using orally administered small molecule JAK inhibitors (JAKi) has garnered much interest in the management of immune-mediated rheumatic diseases, and recently PMR (Table ). Baricitinib, which is a JAK1 and JAK2 inhibitor, exerts a rapid dose-dependent inhibition of IL-6-induced STAT3 phosphorylation, therefore halting the entire subsequent inflammation cascade. Baricitinib was evaluated in the treatment of recent-onset PMR (< 6 months) in the BACHELOR trial, a phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study [ ]. The primary outcome of the study was the attainment of low disease activity, defined as PMR-AS ≤ 10 at week 12, notably without the use of oral GCs. Fourteen (78%) of 18 participants in the baricitinib group achieved this primary outcome compared with 2 (13%) of 15 participants in the placebo group (relative risk 5.8, 95% CI 3.2–10.6; adjusted p < 0.0001) [ ]. The difference in response between the two groups was observed as early as week 2. After week 12, baricitinib dose was reduced from 4 to 2 mg or placebo, for a further 12 weeks, and treatment response was maintained in 16 (89%) of 18 participants. Baricitinib was discontinued at week 24, and during the observational period up to 36 weeks, there were no disease flares. Although promising, these findings require validation in a phase 3 trial, which is currently ongoing (“JAK-SPARE1” EudraCT2020-005081-34). This is particularly important considering that, although patients were required to be GC free in the 2 weeks prior to enrolment, there was no restriction on GC use before this period, and data on cumulative GC exposure prior to enrolment were not reported. Additionally, it should be noted that the trial design permitted subdeltoid GC injections at week 1 and 4, which could have influenced outcomes. Similarly, in the “EAST PMR”, a single-centre, open-label RCT, tofacitinib, a JAK1–3 inhibitor, at 5 mg twice daily, was evaluated as a monotherapy versus oral GCs in treatment-naïve patients with PMR [ ]. At 24 weeks, there was no statistically significant difference in primary outcome between each group, with all patients in both groups achieving a PMR-AS ≤ 10 at 12 and 24 weeks [ ]. Another phase 2 trial ( NCT04799262 ) evaluated tofacitinib at 10 mg per day alongside a GC taper, in both new onset and refractory patients with highly active disease which was defined as a PMR-AS ≥ 17 [ ]. By week 20, 12 of the 14 patients (85.7%) achieved remission ( p = 0.014), defined as a PMR-AS < 7 and a GC dose ≤ 2.5 mg/day (prednisone equivalent) [ ]. The mean GC dose at baseline was 15 mg, which reduced to 1.3 ± 1.2 mg ( p < 0.001) by week 48, and a total of six patients (42.9%) discontinued GC therapy altogether [ ]. A phase 3 RCT, the ITTGPMR study ( NCT06172361 ), is currently ongoing assessing tofacitinib in combination with 4 weeks tapering GCs versus GCs only, in those with high disease activity, defined as a PMR-AS > 10. Whilst these phase 2 trials are promising, JAKi will need to demonstrate a favourable safety profile, especially in this older, vulnerable and comorbid cohort of patients. Although no new safety signals were identified in the above trials, these studies were inadequately powered to investigate the occurrence of major cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, malignancy or serious infection, which, following the post hoc analysis of the ORAL Surveillance trial [ ] and the subsequent warning about JAKi use in elderly patients at

with 4 weeks tapering GCs versus GCs only, in those with high disease activity, defined as a PMR-AS > 10. Whilst these phase 2 trials are promising, JAKi will need to demonstrate a favourable safety profile, especially in this older, vulnerable and comorbid cohort of patients. Although no new safety signals were identified in the above trials, these studies were inadequately powered to investigate the occurrence of major cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, malignancy or serious infection, which, following the post hoc analysis of the ORAL Surveillance trial [ ] and the subsequent warning about JAKi use in elderly patients at higher cardiovascular risk in rheumatoid arthritis, are of concern. Future trials will need to be sufficiently powered, with appropriate follow-up periods, to address such safety concerns, prior to the incorporation of JAKi into the management algorithm for PMR. Interleukin-17 Inhibitors A phase 3 double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT, “REPLENISH” ( NCT05767034 ), is currently ongoing, assessing the efficacy and safety of the IL-17-A antagonist secukinumab in those with relapsing, GC-dependent PMR. Its objective is to evaluate secukinumab at doses of 150 mg or 300 mg every 4 weeks, in combination with a tapering GC regimen. Given the involvement of T helper 17 (TH17) cells in the pathogenesis of PMR [ ] and a promising phase 2 RCT, the TITAIN study ( NCT03765788 ), in GCA [ ], there was much anticipation for the results of REPLENISH. However, Novartis recently announced the failure of secukinumab to show any benefit in either newly diagnosed or patients with relapsing GCA in the phase 3 GCAptAIN trial ( NCT04930094 ). While these results underscore uncertainties regarding its potential role in PMR, further evidence from the REPLENISH trial are eagerly awaited. Antibody Drug Conjugates A recent phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (AIM-PMR study; NCT04972968 ) evaluated a novel antibody–drug conjugate ABBV-154, comprised of adalimumab (a human monoclonal anti-TNFα antagonist) conjugated to a GC receptor modulator (GRM) [ ]. This was developed to mitigate systemic GC-related adverse effects by selectively delivering the GRM to cells that express transmembrane TNF, including activated immune cells [ ]. In total, 181 patients with GC-dependent, refractory PMR were randomised 1:1:1:1 to placebo ( n = 50) or ABBV-154 at 40 mg ( n = 42), 150 mg ( n = 45) or 340 mg ( n = 44) alongside a standardised GC taper [ ]. The primary efficacy endpoint was time to disease flare. The trial was voluntarily terminated early by the sponsor at week 24, as interim analysis determined that the benefit-risk profile did not sufficiently differentiate ABBV-154 from other currently available therapies for PMR. Nonetheless, time to flare at week 24 favoured the ABBV-154 cohort compared to placebo with dose-responsive hazard ratios (HRs): 40 mg, HR 0.49 (95% CI 0.27–0.88; p = 0.017); 150 mg, HR 0.44 (95% CI 0.25–0.79; p = 0.006); 340 mg, HR 0.20 (95% CI 0.09–0.42; p < 0.001) [ ]. Moreover, incidences of treatment emergent adverse events were similar between groups [ ]. Although these findings suggest potential GC-sparing efficacy, interpretation is limited by early termination, reduced exposure time and sample size. Overall, ABBV-154 provides a proof of concept for antibody–drug conjugates in PMR, but confirmatory, adequately powered trials would be required to define clinical utility. Future Perspectives in the Management of PMR While significant strides have been made over the past decade in the management of isolated PMR, in particular the FDA approval of the first biologic therapy, sarilumab for use in refractory disease, substantial uncertainties remain. Relative to PMRs prevalence, associated disability and significant impact on HRQoL, the progress in management remains inadequate. Indeed, the research agenda and knowledge gaps continue to expand, highlighting persistent knowledge gaps across diagnosis, disease monitoring and optimal treatment strategies. The precise role of the rheumatologist in the care of those with PMR is an ongoing matter of debate. Whilst the importance of specialist evaluation and the benefit of rapid access referral pathways are clear, the practicalities of increased resources for PMR in an already strained rheumatology workforce remain uncertain. However, with an increasing number of biologic agents under evaluation, and the anticipated evolving therapeutic landscape, the need for specialist input will become even more relevant. More studies evaluating the utility, feasibility and cost-effectiveness of early specialist input with rapid access services in ensuring enhanced short- and long-term outcomes including an accurate diagnosis, instigation of appropriate early therapy, stratification for GC sparing agents as appropriate and minimisation of GC-related adverse events are required. However, in order to optimise the role of the rheumatologist, there is an urgent need for the development of a disease stratification tool. In addition to serological or imaging biomarkers, future research should explore the potential of a multimodal prognostication tool including clinical and demographic features, serological and imaging markers, and PROMs. Indeed, the

studies evaluating the utility, feasibility and cost-effectiveness of early specialist input with rapid access services in ensuring enhanced short- and long-term outcomes including an accurate diagnosis, instigation of appropriate early therapy, stratification for GC sparing agents as appropriate and minimisation of GC-related adverse events are required. However, in order to optimise the role of the rheumatologist, there is an urgent need for the development of a disease stratification tool. In addition to serological or imaging biomarkers, future research should explore the potential of a multimodal prognostication tool including clinical and demographic features, serological and imaging markers, and PROMs. Indeed, the role of PROMs in PMR management needs greater attention in future studies and RCTs. There is a need for clear therapeutic algorithms to guide the management of both early and refractory PMR, along with consensus recommendations for optimal management at each stage of the disease. The potential of a GC-free management in early PMR may be feasible, as demonstrated in the promising results of the BACHELOR RCT [ ]. However, these findings need to be validated in a phase 3 trial, and the roles of other biological therapies in this context also warrant further investigation. Although both biologic agents and JAKi are currently more expensive than oral GCs, the emergence of biosimilars and low cost generics may reduce cost barriers. When considered alongside improved efficacy and safety profiles, particularly in terms of reducing cumulative GC exposure and associated adverse effects, the early, upfront use of these therapies may become a justified and practical approach in future PMR management. Additionally, we know that many GC-dependent patients with PMR are often not considered for management escalation or a GC-sparing agent [ ]. There is perhaps an inertia when the maintenance GC dose is deemed to be relatively low; however, we need to adapt the same standards to GCs in PMR as we do in our other inflammatory rheumatic diseases. The current guidance on monitoring and managing GC-induced adverse events is vague, resulting in much ambiguity and resultant failure to implement appropriate strategies. Finally, there is a need to intensify translational research. Our current understanding of the pathophysiology of PMR is limited, and in order to guide the development and evaluation of targeted therapeutics, greater clarity on the pathogenetic mechanisms is urgently required. Conclusion Despite a recent resurgence of interest in PMR within the rheumatology community and literature, isolated PMR management remains underrepresented in the research landscape compared to other immune-mediated rheumatic disease of a similar prevalence. Critical knowledge gaps persist, particularly in the areas of diagnosis, disease monitoring and long-term management. In this context, we have underscored the importance of early rheumatology input, the development of evidence-based diagnostic tools and prognostic markers, improved monitoring strategies, and approaches to minimise GC exposure and associated adverse effects. With the expanding therapeutic horizon, including the emergence of effective GC-sparing agents, these priorities are increasingly relevant to improve overall outcomes in those with PMR.

documents.title: ACR EULAR classification criteria primary Sjogren syndrome anti-SSA

chunks.content: Sjögren’s syndrome (SS) is a multisystem autoimmune disease characterized by hypofunction of salivary and lacrimal glands and possible systemic multi-organ manifestations. It is primarily overseen by rheumatologists, in collaboration with ophthalmologists and oral medicine/pathology specialists. None of the 11 classification/diagnostic criteria published for SS from 1965 to 2002,( – ) had been endorsed by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) or European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR). During the past decade, the most commonly used classification criteria have been the American European Consensus Group (AECG) criteria,( ) which have proven useful in research and clinical practice. In 2012, new classification criteria developed within the NIH-funded Sjögren’s International Collaborative Clinical Alliance (SICCA) registry were published after being provisionally approved by ACR.( ) These criteria were designed for entry into clinical trials, and the target population used for their development and validation consisted of individuals with signs and symptoms suggestive of SS. Subsequent analyses to compare the ACR and AECG criteria performed in a cohort of patients at the Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation (OMRF) revealed a high level of concordance.( ) Although both criteria sets involve similar items, the AECG criteria allow substitutions for alternatives and the use of symptoms of dry eyes and mouth in classifying patients. The provisional ACR criteria are based solely on objective tests, and consider symptoms as inclusion criteria for the target population to whom the criteria should apply. While some treatments may improve symptoms and prevent complications of SS, currently there is no cure. However, the recent development of new therapeutic options for the management of various autoimmune diseases is promising for SS patients. Well-defined entry criteria, and endpoints that allow measurement of the effect of new treatments are needed for the development of new therapies. Disease activity indices for SS endpoints have recently been developed and validated by the EULAR Sjögren’s Task Force: EULAR SS Patient Reported Index (ESSPRI) and EULAR SS Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI).( – ) The need for international consensus on classification criteria has recently been recognized by the SS scientific community.( ) Furthermore, this international criteria set should be established using guidelines published by both ACR and EULAR in order to be approved by both organizations.( , ) In 2012, investigators from the SICCA team and the EULAR Sjögren’s Task Force formed the International SS Criteria Working Group. The objective was to develop classification criteria for primary SS (pSS) that combined features of the ACR and AECG criteria, using methods consistent with ACR and EULAR guidelines. We describe here the development and validation of the resulting criteria, which have been approved by the ACR and EULAR. Consistent with our goal of producing criteria to aid in recruitment for clinical trials, we focus on primary rather than secondary SS. Patients with the latter would typically not be eligible for experimental treatments for SS. METHODS Overview Our methods rely on both data and expert clinical judgment, and mirror those used for the development and validation of the 2010 ACR-EULAR criteria for rheumatoid arthritis,( ) and the 2013 ACR-EULAR criteria for systemic sclerosis.( ) The approach is outlined below ( ): A preliminary list of candidate items was generated based on the AECG and ACR criteria, and guided by analyses of existing datasets (item generation). This list was finalized in two meetings of the International SS Criteria Working Group, held concurrently with the 2013 International Symposium on SS and the 2013 ACR meeting. We used multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA)( ) to reduce the number of candidate criteria items, assign preliminary weights (item reduction and weight assignment), and help define a draft criteria set. We tested and adapted the draft criteria using a development cohort with pSS disease status derived from expert clinical judgment based on clinical vignettes. We then tested the performance of the classification criteria in a similarly defined but separate validation cohort of patients. We also tested the performance of the classification criteria in a subset of difficult cases as described below. International SS Criteria Working Group The working group comprised 55 clinician-experts including 36 rheumatologists, 10 oral medicine/pathology specialists, and 9 ophthalmologists; and two patient advocates (from the USA and Europe). The methodology team consisted of a statistician (SCS) and two epidemiologists (CHS and RS). Approximately half of the clinician-experts were from Europe (Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the UK), and among the other half, most were from North and South America (the USA and Argentina), with the remaining from Japan. Item generation Extensive statistical analyses were performed within the SICCA dataset with input from the working group to better understand the similarities and differences between the AECG and ACR criteria sets. Concomitantly, statistical analyses were performed within the OMRF cohort comparing the ACR and the AECG criteria, and a high level of concordance was identified (91%

(CHS and RS). Approximately half of the clinician-experts were from Europe (Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the UK), and among the other half, most were from North and South America (the USA and Argentina), with the remaining from Japan. Item generation Extensive statistical analyses were performed within the SICCA dataset with input from the working group to better understand the similarities and differences between the AECG and ACR criteria sets. Concomitantly, statistical analyses were performed within the OMRF cohort comparing the ACR and the AECG criteria, and a high level of concordance was identified (91% concordance among 646 OMRF participants, including 244 who met both sets of criteria and 343 who did not meet either).( ) Considering the high level of concordance observed between the AECG and ACR criteria, and the fact that the components in both criteria sets overlap to some degree, there was general agreement on many of the key items for inclusion. However, some tests were included in the AECG but not in the ACR criteria (the Schirmer test, unstimulated whole saliva (UWS) flow rate, sialography, salivary scintigraphy), and others were included in the ACR but not in the AECG criteria (the antinuclear/ANA antibody titer and rheumatoid factor/RF). Also, the ocular dryness was measured using the van Bijsterveld score (VBS) in the AECG criteria, and the Ocular Staining Score (OSS) in the ACR criteria, although these tests both measure ocular staining, the former with lissamine green and the latter with lissamine green (for conjunctiva) and fluorescein (for cornea). The comparative analyses performed both in the SICCA and OMRF cohorts, and presented to the working group, guided the generation of a final list of candidate items. It was agreed that all items originally included in both AECG and ACR criteria, except for ANA titer and RF, would be initial candidate items. The decision to exclude ANA and RF was based on analyses that revealed that an extremely small number of cases who met the ACR criteria were anti-SSA/B(Ro/La) negative but ANA (titer ≥ 1:320) and RF positive.( ) Item reduction and weight assignment Relative ranking of selected items reflecting clinician-expert opinions was based on a web-based MCDA survey administered using 1000Minds software.( , ) This approach, based on pairwise ranking of alternatives, each defined using selected criteria items, has been described.( ) The resulting item weights were normalized as percentages, and used to define an additive score (described below) reflecting the likelihood of assigning disease case status. Development and validation patient cohorts Three prospective cohorts of individuals with signs and symptoms suggestive of SS have been recruited over the past 10 years by teams who are now members of the International SS Criteria Working Group. These include 1) the SICCA cohort, comprised of 3514 participants (including 1578 individuals who meet the ACR classification criteria for pSS) recruited from Argentina, China, Denmark, India, Japan, the UK and the USA (co-principal investigators (PIs): C. Shiboski and L. Criswell, at the University of California San Francisco); 2) the Paris-Sud cohort that includes 1011 participants (including 440 individuals who meet the AECG criteria for pSS) recruited in Paris, France (PI: X. Mariette at Paris-Sud University, Bicêtre hospital in Paris); and 3) the OMRF cohort, that includes 837 participants (including 279 individuals who meet the AECG criteria for pSS) evaluated at either the Sjögren’s Research Clinic at OMRF or the Sjögren’s Clinic in the University of Minnesota (PI: K. Sivils,OMRF). These cohorts share several key characteristics that make them appropriate for criteria development: Inclusion criteria required that participants have signs and symptoms suggestive of SS, warranting a comprehensive work-up by a multi-disciplinary team of SS clinicians. In addition to symptom-related data, objective tests with respect to oral, ocular, and systemic/serological endpoints had been collected using similar procedures: Oral tests: labial salivary gland (LSG) biopsy to identify focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (FLS) and focus score (FS)( ); UWS flow rates.( , ) Ocular tests: OSS using lissamine green and fluorescein, and other ocular tests such as Schirmer test and tear break-up time. For the ocular staining test, the Paris-Sud cohort used the VBS,( ) while SICCA used the OSS,( ) and OMRF used both. The Paris-Sud cohort also used fluorescein and collected data on the individual OSS components, so it could be computed subsequently. Thus data from the Paris-Sud and OMRF cohorts could be analyzed to establish a conversion algorithm between both scores as follows: for lower scores, 1–3, the VBS was equal to the OSS, but VBS of 4, 5, or 6 were equivalent to OSS scores of 5, 6, or 7, respectively. For the clinical vignettes, the ocular staining test was expressed as the OSS ranging from 0 to 7 and above. A group of four ophthalmologists from France, the US, and the UK formed an ad-hoc working

and collected data on the individual OSS components, so it could be computed subsequently. Thus data from the Paris-Sud and OMRF cohorts could be analyzed to establish a conversion algorithm between both scores as follows: for lower scores, 1–3, the VBS was equal to the OSS, but VBS of 4, 5, or 6 were equivalent to OSS scores of 5, 6, or 7, respectively. For the clinical vignettes, the ocular staining test was expressed as the OSS ranging from 0 to 7 and above. A group of four ophthalmologists from France, the US, and the UK formed an ad-hoc working group that interpreted the analyses performed on the Paris-Sud data (ML and TML) and on the OMRF data (AR). Together, they derived the conversion algorithm between the OSS and the VBS described above. In addition, since the VBS of 4 (previously used in the AECG criteria) was equivalent to an OSS of 5, the group agreed to modify the OSS threshold to 5 in the new criteria set. This threshold has also been shown, as part of subsequent analyses of the SICCA data, to be more specific for diagnostic purposes than the previous score of 3 (data not shown). Serological assays: including anti-SSA/B(Ro/La), ANA titers, RF, IgG, presence of complement C3 and C4. Cohort PIs were each asked to provide a dataset that consisted of a random sample of 400 individuals with equal numbers of pSS cases and non-cases (using their own diagnostic definition), and without revealing case status in the dataset. The combined datasets thus comprised 1200 individuals with well-characterized data on the phenotypic features of SS. Clinical vignettes describing each individual’s relevant features in text form were computer-generated using a program written in R version 3.2.( ) Vignettes described each individual with respect to age, gender, reported symptoms, clinical signs, and provided test results including ANA titers, RF, IgG, C3, C4, anti-SSA(Ro), anti-SSB(La), OSS for each eye, Schirmer for each eye, whether or not the LSG biopsy revealed FLS, and a FS ( ). Ocular symptoms were defined according to the AECG definition, as a positive response to at least one of the following questions: 1) Have you had daily, persistent, troublesome dry eyes for more than 3 months? 2) Do you have a recurrent sensation of sand or gravel in the eyes? 3) Do you use tear substitutes more than 3 times a day? Oral symptoms were defined as a positive response to at least one of the following questions: 1) Have you had a daily feeling of dry mouth for more than 3 months? 2) Do you frequently drink liquids to aid in swallowing dry food? Assessment of SS case/control status We excluded 4 vignettes selected randomly from the study population to obtain 1196 vignettes that were randomly distributed into 26 surveys, each containing 46 individual vignettes. Research Electonic Data Capture (REDCap),( ) was used to administer each survey blindly to two clinician-experts. Twenty six pairs of clinician-experts participated in the first survey exercise, and each pair completed one survey. They were instructed to review each vignette, and asked if they thought the patient described had pSS. Responses included: “yes”, “no”, and “not sure”. Concordant yes/no responses were used to assign case/non-case status; concordant “not sure” responses were interpreted as non-gradable vignettes. All vignettes with discordant answers (yes/no; yes/not sure; or no/not sure) were included in a second round of surveys that were each sent to a third clinician-expert (a total of nine clinician-experts contributed to the second round of surveys). Concordance was then defined as two concordant answers out of three with a vignette defined as a pSS case if the answers included two “yes”. Similarly, a vignette was defined as a non-SS control if the answers included two “no”. The vignettes which received three discordant answers (yes/no/not sure) were considered “difficult cases”, and were combined into a third survey sent to eight clinician-experts, members of the steering committee. These difficult cases were defined as SS cases if the majority of clinician-experts (five out of eight) responded “yes” to a vignette, and as non-SS controls if the majority (five out of eight) responded “no”. Randomization of vignettes across development and validation cohorts Each of the 1196 vignettes was assigned a unique identification number (ID), and were randomly divided into two groups of 598, one to be used as development cohort, and the other for validation purposes. Clinician-experts who completed the surveys were blinded to the origin (development or validation set) of the clinical vignettes. Results were summarized graphically, and using summary statistics. Clinician-experts who completed the surveys were blinded to the origin (development or validation set) of the clinical vignettes. Testing and adaptation of the draft criteria We conducted exploratory analyses of the clinician-expert rankings derived from the MCDA survey to characterize distributions of item-specific weights. Results were summarized graphically, and using summary statistics. We also performed analyses linking vignette items from the development cohort with corresponding clinician-expert outcome classifications, restricted to individuals with clinician-expert-assigned case/non-case outcomes. Conditional random forest classifiers( ) were used to obtain variable importance rankings for (1) all vignette items, and (2) binary indicators corresponding to the items and used in the MCDA survey. Based on results from exploratory analyses, we defined several candidate classification criteria focusing the items selected by clinician-experts for the MCDA survey. Criteria were defined based on scores computed as weighted sums of binary indicators of presence/absence of items, with weights reflecting relative importance. In addition to the MCDA-derived weights, we used logistic regression models fitted to the development sample to derive alternate weights from item-specific coefficients. Cut-off values for case designation for candidate criteria were computed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) methods applied to clinician-expert-defined outcomes in the development dataset. For each candidate, two cut-off values were identified using a generalized Youden index.( ) The first weighted sensitivity and specificity as equally important, and the second weighted specificity as twice as important as sensitivity. We held a final meeting of the SS Working Group to present and discuss testing and adaptation of the draft criteria results. A summary report was subsequently sent to all members, including those who could not attend the meeting. A REDCap survey was administered to the entire panel of clinician-experts, seeking consensus on the final draft criteria prior to validation. Validation Validation of candidate criteria was based on ROC analyses using the validation sample, restricted to individuals with clinician-expert-assigned case/non-case outcomes. We separately assessed classification performance in the subset of difficult cases. Performance was summarized using estimated sensitivity and specificity with accompanying 95% confidence intervals, and area under the curve (AUC) statistics. RESULTS MCDA survey: distribution of responses and item weights Fifty-two clinician-experts participated in the MCDA survey. presents the item weights for each of the seven items. Note that weights are normalized to sum to 1, yielding a proportion interpretation. presents the distribution of item weights across experts. The curves in the figure are smoothed kernel density estimates that have a relative frequency interpretation similar to histograms. Results indicate that an LSG biopsy result of FLS with FS ≥ 1 and anti-SSA/B(Ro/La) positivity received the highest average weights, followed by OSS, UWS, Schirmer, oral symptoms and ocular symptoms, respectively. Weight distributions for ocular/oral symptoms, Schirmer/UWS and FS/anti-SSA/B(Ro/La) were remarkably similar in both mode and variability. Case status assessment in development and validation cohorts The first round of surveys yielded 819 concordant and 377 discordant responses ( ). The concordant responses provided 415 pSS cases and 377 non-SS controls. The 377 vignettes with discordant responses were included in a second round of nine surveys assigned to nine clinician-experts, providing a third response to each discordant vignette. This yielded an additional 151 pSS cases and 125 non-SS controls (with two out of three concordant responses). When reconciling ID numbers among the vignettes initially randomly assigned to be used in either cohort, the first two rounds of surveys yielded 288 pSS cases and 248 non-SS controls in the development cohort, and 278 pSS cases and 254 non-SS controls in the validation cohort. The 72 vignettes in the second round of survey that received three discordant responses were included in a third round of surveys administered to the eight members of the steering committee who were also clinician-experts. These provided a pool of 49 difficult cases that received a majority of concordant responses (5/8) after the third round of survey: 35 pSS cases and 14 non-SS controls. Criteria development Random forest variable importance rankings based on the clinician-expert classifications of the development dataset vignettes are shown in . Results based on all vignette variables, as well as the binary indicators consistent with items included in the MCDA survey are shown. Rankings agree well with results from the MCDA survey, and clearly indicate the relatively greater importance of objective measures such as the LSG FS and antibody results in expert classification decisions. Oral and ocular symptoms did not affect classification performance, reflecting the observation that over 94% of individuals had at least one symptom. An initial criteria score was developed as a weighted sum of the 7 items in the MCDA survey, based on the average weights reported in . We used

Rankings agree well with results from the MCDA survey, and clearly indicate the relatively greater importance of objective measures such as the LSG FS and antibody results in expert classification decisions. Oral and ocular symptoms did not affect classification performance, reflecting the observation that over 94% of individuals had at least one symptom. An initial criteria score was developed as a weighted sum of the 7 items in the MCDA survey, based on the average weights reported in . We used logistic regression models to develop an alternate empirical criteria score for the development data, focusing on the items used in the MCDA survey, but including indicators for anti-SSA(Ro) and anti-SSB(La) positivity as separate variables. Scores were computed using weights based on rescaled regression coefficients from a model retaining items representing significant predictors of case status.( ) Oral and ocular symptoms, and anti-SSB(La) positivity were excluded because they did not affect classification performance based on the random forest variable importance rankings from the clinician-expert classifications of the development dataset vignettes ( ). Furthermore, oral and/or ocular symptoms had been used among inclusion criteria for participation in the three patient cohorts, and therefore a group decision was made that oral and/or ocular symptoms or suspicion of SS based on one of the domains of ESSDAI would be preliminary requirements for applying the new SS classification criteria. The decision to exclude anti-SSB(La) as an item was also based on group discussions and on a study published by Baer and colleagues( ) that demonstrated that the presence of anti-SSB(La) without anti-SSA(Ro) antibodies, had no significant association with SS phenotypic features, relative to seronegative participants. ROC analysis of the MCDA score yielded an AUC of 0.96, and two alternate cut-offs for case classification ( ), ROC analysis of the logistic score yielded an AUC value of 0.98, and two alternate cut-offs for case classification. We also considered a modified version of the logistic score that assigned equal weights to the OSS, Schirmer and UWS items, reflecting clinician-expert opinions that UWS should be weighted similarly to the Schirmer test, and for greater consistency with the results of the MCDA survey ( ). The ROC analysis yielded similar results to the logistic score (AUC=0.98; ). also presents kappa statistics measuring agreement between outcome classifications based on the three alternative criterion scores and classifications with the existing AECG and ACR criteria. Results indicate high levels of agreement, with the strongest values obtained from the logistic and modified logistic scores with a cut-off selected to weigh sensitivity and specificity equally. The REDCap survey seeking consensus on the final draft criteria, yielded 98% clinician-expert-consensus towards the modified logistic score as the basis for final draft criteria, with case status based on a score ≥ 4, and agreement to move forward with validation of these criteria. presents the final criteria definition. Criteria validation We compared the validation and development data with respect to key variables, including their associations with outcome classification. Overall agreement was quite high, indicating no major differences apparent in the two datasets ( ). Initial validation of the selected criteria was based on estimated sensitivity and specificity using the clinician-expert responses in the full validation dataset. Sensitivity was 96% (95% CI: 92%, 98%), and specificity was 95% (95% CI: 92%, 97%). Validation was also performed in the subset of 49 difficult cases and non-cases, for which sensitivity was 83% (95% CI: 66%, 93%), and specificity was 100% (95% CI: 77%, 100%). DISCUSSION We present an international set of classification criteria for pSS, developed and validated using approaches approved by both ACR and EULAR committees that oversee classification criteria. These criteria are applicable to any patient with at least one symptom of ocular or oral dryness (based on AECG questions),( ) or suspicion of SS due to systemic features derived from the ESSDAI( ) measure with at least one positive domain item. The criteria do not apply to anyone with a prior diagnosis of a pre-specified list of conditions that would exclude participation in pSS therapeutic trials because of overlapping clinical features or interference with criteria tests. The new classification criteria are based on five objective tests/items, and a total score ≥ 4, derived from the sum of the weights assigned to each positive test/item: with FLS with FS ≥ 1 and positive anti-SSA(Ro) serology having the highest weights (3 each) and OSS ≥ 5 (or VBS ≥ 4) on at least one eye, Schirmer test ≤ 5 mm/5min on at least one eye, and UWS flow rate ≤ 0.1 mL/min, having a weight of 1 each. We found that the criteria perform very well when validated using vignettes derived from patients with pSS status defined by expert opinion.

classification criteria are based on five objective tests/items, and a total score ≥ 4, derived from the sum of the weights assigned to each positive test/item: with FLS with FS ≥ 1 and positive anti-SSA(Ro) serology having the highest weights (3 each) and OSS ≥ 5 (or VBS ≥ 4) on at least one eye, Schirmer test ≤ 5 mm/5min on at least one eye, and UWS flow rate ≤ 0.1 mL/min, having a weight of 1 each. We found that the criteria perform very well when validated using vignettes derived from patients with pSS status defined by expert opinion. The criteria retained high sensitivity and specificity in a subset of 49 difficult cases/non-cases. The form of the proposed criteria improve upon previous criteria, in that they are based on a weighted sum of items, with weights derived from consensus expert opinion and analyses of patient data. Also, positive serology for anti-SSB/(La) in the absence of anti-SSA(Ro) is no longer considered a criteria item. For instance, in the validation cohort, 15 individuals were anti-SSB(La)-positive in the absence of anti-SSA(Ro) and FLS in the LSG biopsy, thus would have been classified as non-SS using the new criteria. However, 12 of these would have tested positive based on both the AECG and 2012 ACR criteria, and would very likely have been misclassified. Improvements from the 2012-ACR criteria include the addition of the Schirmer test and the UWS, the use of a higher threshold for the OSS (≥ 5) and the optional use of the VBS as an alternative to the OSS (in cases where an ophthalmologist trained in the OSS is not available). Additional modifications include removal of the high-titer ANA and positive RF as items. Improvements from the 2002-AECG criteria include oral and ocular symptoms being considered part of eligibility determination rather than serving as items, the OSS being included as an alternative to the VBS, sialography and salivary scintigraphy being omitted. Furthermore, the new criteria consider systemic signs and B-cell activation biomarkers (using the ESSDAI) as inclusion criteria, which will allow diagnosis of systemic and earlier forms of the disease when sicca features are not already present. Compared with the AECG criteria, exclusionary conditions have also been updated. IgG4-related disease was added, HCV infection is restricted to patients with positive PCR, and pre-existing lymphoma is allowable, since diagnosis of SS is sometimes made after a prior lymphoma occurrence. Strengths of our approach include 1) assignment of criteria item weights combined consensus methods for quantifying expert opinion with confirmatory statistical analysis of real patient vignettes classified by clinician-experts; 2) the working group was international, and represented a range of clinical specialties (65% rheumatologists, 18% oral medicine/pathology specialists, and 16% ophthalmologists); 3) our methods have been successfully applied in the development and validation of ACR/EULAR classification criteria for RA( ) and systemic sclerosis.( ) Another advantage of these methods is that they are adaptable to future modifications of the criteria that may arise with the adoption of new diagnostic tests, such as parotid ultrasonography, or improved serological assays. For example, some research suggests that it may be important to distinguish between monospecific antibody assays to Ro60 or Ro52,( – ) although further validation studies will be required before they can be used for patient classification. A shared limitation, common to criteria for many rheumatic diseases, is the use of expert clinical judgement in the absence of an objective "gold standard" for defining the disease, and the associated effect of the resulting "circularity" on measured performance of criteria sets. The primary application of classification criteria is recruitment into clinical trials and studies. Although our study focused on classification of pSS, the proposed criteria may be applicable to SS associated with other autoimmune diseases. However, further research is needed to confirm this. The landscape of SS has changed in recent years, due to both the recently validated disease activity indices, and the availability of new therapeutic agents. Using methodology consistent with other recent ACR/EULAR-approved classification criteria, we developed a single set of data-driven consensus classification criteria for pSS, that performed well in validation, and are well-suited as entry criteria for clinical trials.
