When considering these cases as negative, the sensitivity and specificity for histological diagnosis were as follows: 69.1% (95% CI, 61.7%-74.6%) and 99.2% (95% CI, 92.2%-99.3%), respectively. It is worth mentioning that the diagnostic sensitivity of histology was complete agreement with cytology ( P = 1). Furthermore, when combining cytology and histology, the diagnostic sensitivity and specificity were 73.6% (95% CI, 66.4%–79.8%) and 98.3% (95% CI, 93.4%–99.7%), respectively. No statistically significant differences in diagnostic sensitivity were observed when compared with either cytology alone ( P = 0.348) or histology ( P = 0.554) at this stage [Table ]. In addition, we evaluated the diagnostic performance of various combinations of diagnostic tests [Table ]. For the 64 patients who underwent concurrent ERCP-based brush cytology, the results showed a diagnostic sensitivity of 50% (95% CI, 34.8%–65.2%) and specificity of 95% (95% CI, 73.1%–100%). Similarly, among the 57 patients who underwent concurrent ERCP-based transpapillary biopsy sampling, the diagnostic sensitivity was 70% (95% CI, 50.4%–84.6%), and specificity was 96.3% (95% CI, 79.1%–99.8%). Notably, in 32 patients who underwent both brush cytology and transpapillary biopsy simultaneously, diagnostic performance significantly improved, yielding a sensitivity of 77.8% (95% CI, 51.9%–92.6%) and specificity of 100% (95% CI, 73.2%–100%). Further enhancement of diagnostic accuracy was observed in 30 patients who underwent simultaneous collection of all 4 pathologic specimens, with diagnostic sensitivity reaching 88.2% (95% CI, 62.3%–97.9%) and specificity at 92.3% (95% CI, 62.1%–99.6%). Subgroup analysis The analysis was meticulously stratified based on the primary pathogenetic cause of DBSs [Table ]. Notably, when we considered the anatomical location of the primary lesions, we found that the sensitivity of EUS-FNA cytology for lesions in the bile ducts, pancreas, and duodenal papilla was 69.4% (95% CI, 57.3%–79.5%), 70.5% (95% CI, 59%–80%), and 69.2% (95% CI, 48.1%–84.9%), respectively. The corresponding specificity values were 98.7% (95% CI, 91.8%–100%), 100% (95% CI, 82.1%–100%), and 94.4% (95% CI, 70.6%–99.7%). Meanwhile, the diagnostic sensitivity of EUS-FNA histology for detecting lesions at these same sites was as follows: 75.4% (95% CI, 62.9%–84.9%) for bile ducts, 74.6% (95% CI, 62.7%–83.9%) for the pancreas, and 79.2% (95% CI, 57.3%–92.1%) for the duodenal papilla. Specificity values remained consistently high at 98.6% (95% CI, 91.7%–100%), 100% (95% CI, 81.5%–100%), and 94.4% (95% CI, 70.6%–99.7%). Furthermore, when combining EUS-FNA cytology and EUS-FNA histology, we observed improved diagnostic sensitivity for lesions at these anatomical sites, with values of 80% (95% CI, 67.9%–88.5%), 83.1% (95% CI, 71.9%–90.6%), and 83.3% (95% CI, 61.8%–94.5%), respectively. Importantly, specificity values remained consistently high at 98.6% (95% CI, 91.7%–100%), 100% (95% CI, 81.5%–100%), and 94.4% (95% CI, 70.6%–99.7%). Although diagnostic sensitivity appeared higher for lesions with primary disease located around the pancreas and duodenum compared with those in the bile ducts, these differences did not attain statistical significance. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on pertinent imaging manifestations observed in CT or magnetic resonance imaging scans for cases of DBSs [Table ]. These analyses considered factors such as the presence of a mass, maximum diameter of upstream bile duct dilatation, presence of truncation, and the size of the mass area. Notably, the diagnostic sensitivity of EUS-FNA cytology exhibited significant variation based on the presence of a mass shadow. Specifically, the sensitivity was notably higher in cases with a discernible mass shadow compared with those without (75.9% vs. 57.4%, P = 0.011). Furthermore, when combining cytology with histology, the diagnostic sensitivity remained significantly higher in the presence of a mass shadow (85.8% vs. 72.7%, P = 0.043). However, there was no such difference in the sensitivity of histology alone (79.2% vs. 67.3%, P = 0.095). Notably, the size of the mass also exerted an influence on the diagnostic sensitivity of cytology. Specifically, when the mass area was greater than or equal to 9.5 cm 2 , the diagnostic sensitivity was significantly higher compared with cases with a mass area less than 9.5 cm 2 (85.4% vs. 66.7%, P = 0.046). Additionally, the diagnostic tendencies of specialized imaging physicians significantly impacted the sensitivity of cytology diagnosis. Cytology exhibited a diagnostic sensitivity of only 51.9% (95% CI, 38%–65.5%) for lesions that were not definitively diagnosed by imaging. In cases where the imaging diagnosis leaned toward a benign interpretation (63.6%) or a malignant tendency (78.2%), statistically significant differences were observed ( P = 0.002). However, it is worth noting that there were no significant differences in the diagnostic sensitivity of EUS-FNA puncture pathology when subgroups were analyzed based on factors such as the presence of comorbidities (eg, acute pancreatitis, acute cholangitis, choledochal stones), the thickness of the puncture needles, the manufacturer of the operative equipment, the duration of the EUS-FNA operation, and the proficiency of the operator [Table ]. In addition, refer to Supplemental Table 1, http://links.lww.com/ENUS/A363 , for the basic information, laboratory test results, imaging data, and surgical details of patients using different EUS-FNA puncture needles. IgG4-related disease Among our cohort of 118 patients diagnosed with benign DBSs, a notable subset of 33 individuals (28%) received a diagnosis of IgG4-RD. Of these cases, 26 were male patients, whereas the remaining 7 were female patients, with male patients averaging 60.73 years in age and female patients averaging 64.46 years [Table ]. In terms of disease manifestation, we observed that 20 cases exhibited involvement in a single region, including the head and neck, chest, hepatobiliary pancreas, or retroperitoneum. Thirteen cases presented with multiple region involvement, and intriguingly, 9 male patients displayed involvement across multiple regions. Serum IgG4 levels in patients diagnosed with IgG4-RD exhibited a mean value of 8.69 g/L. Notably, IgG4 levels fell within the normal range for 4 cases, were 1 to 2 times the upper limit in 8 patients and 2 to 5 times the upper limit in 12 patients, and exceeded 5 times the upper limit in 9 cases. In comparison with other etiologies of DBSs, it is significant to highlight that patients with IgG4-RD presented elevated transaminase and bilirubin levels ( P < 0.05). Moreover, tumor marker levels demonstrated a notable elevation in IgG4-RDs, with a median CA-199 level of 69.30 U/L. [Table ]. Radiological imaging of the biliopancreatic system among patients with IgG4-RDs in our study consistently revealed diffuse pancreatic swelling, suspicious thickening of the wall of the pancreatic segment of the common bile duct, luminal stenosis, dilatation of the upstream bile ducts, and diffuse swelling in other regions. Positron emission tomography/CT scans further suggested nodular increases in FDG metabolism [Figure ]. It is noteworthy that histopathologic specimens of the pancreaticobiliary duct obtained by EUS-FNA puncture in only 9 patients showed histopathologic manifestations typical or partially typical of IgG4-RD (dense lymphocytic infiltrate and storiform fibrosis with or without obliterative phlebitis; the IgG4 + :IgG + ratio is ≥41%, and/or the number of IgG4 + cells/high-power field is ≥10) [Figure ]. DISCUSSION Indeterminate DBSs present a diagnostic challenge. We examined EUS-FNA cytology and histology for suspected malignant DBSs in this study. The sensitivity of EUS-FNA cytology, histology, and codiagnosis was 69.1%, 76.4%, and 82%, respectively, and the diagnostic sensitivity was 97.5%, 99.1%, and 99.1%, respectively. The diagnostic efficacy, in terms of both sensitivity and specificity, remained consistent for EUS-FNA cytology and histology, irrespective of considering instances of histological slide failure. Furthermore, the origin of DBSs—whether stemming from bile duct, pancreatic, or duodenal papillary lesions—did not significantly impact the diagnostic efficacy of EUS-FNA. Interestingly, we observed heightened diagnostic efficacy associated with EUS-FNA in cases where a discernible mass shadow surrounded the DBSs, particularly when this shadow exhibited larger dimensions. Additionally, benign DBSs due to IgG4-RDs accounted for 28% of cases, a crucial factor in the differential diagnosis. Numerous studies have addressed DBSs, yet varying anatomical definitions persist. Commonly used delineations encompass the distal third of the extrahepatic bile duct, the intrapancreatic segment of the common bile duct, or the distal half of the extrahepatic bile duct. [ – ] In this article, we adopt a precise definition for distal bile duct stricture: the bile ducts distal to the posterior duodenum and proximal to the confluence of the cystic duct with the common bile duct. This definition aligns with that of distal CCA in the joint manual of cancer staging issued by the American Joint Committee on Cancer and the Union for International Cancer Control. [ ] Its anatomical clarity simplifies clinical application. For DBSs, selecting the appropriate tissue acquisition method is crucial. ERCP-guided tissue acquisition is recommended when biliary drainage is necessary. [ ] However, when cross-sectional imaging indicates a mass associated with the stricture or when ERCP-guided tissue acquisition fails, EUS-FNA becomes the preferred option. [ ] In our study, about 20% of patients required ERCP for biliary stent placement or endoscopic nasobiliary drainage for drainage. Sensitivities for ERCP-guided brushings, biopsies, and combined brushings and biopsies in this group were 50%, 70%, and 77.8%, respectively. These results align with the diagnostic sensitivity range (43%–81%) reported in existing literature for ERCP. [ – ] In contrast, EUS-FNA offers distinct advantages, particularly in diagnosing mass-type lesions, which are prevalent in

drainage is necessary. [ ] However, when cross-sectional imaging indicates a mass associated with the stricture or when ERCP-guided tissue acquisition fails, EUS-FNA becomes the preferred option. [ ] In our study, about 20% of patients required ERCP for biliary stent placement or endoscopic nasobiliary drainage for drainage. Sensitivities for ERCP-guided brushings, biopsies, and combined brushings and biopsies in this group were 50%, 70%, and 77.8%, respectively. These results align with the diagnostic sensitivity range (43%–81%) reported in existing literature for ERCP. [ – ] In contrast, EUS-FNA offers distinct advantages, particularly in diagnosing mass-type lesions, which are prevalent in DBSs with a primary pancreatic etiology. Among 146 patients with imaging suggestive of a mass shadow, EUS-FNA cytology, histology, and combined cytology and histology demonstrated diagnostic sensitivities of 75.9%, 79.2%, and 85.8%, respectively—outperforming cases with solely bile duct stricture on imaging. This finding corroborates previous studies. In a meta-analysis of 4 studies encompassing 158 patients, EUS-FNA exhibited a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 83% (95% CI, 68%–98%) and 100% (95% CI, 63%–100%) for DBSs, comparable to our study’s sensitivity (82%) and specificity (99.1%) for EUS-FNA cytology combined with histology in DBS diagnosis. [ ] Notably, EUS-FNA’s diagnostic performance excels in identifying pancreatic masses, with pooled sensitivity and specificity of 86.8% and 95.8% in a meta-analysis. [ ] In cases of biliary stricture, EUS-FNA yields a sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 97% for characterizing the stricture. [ ] These findings underscore EUS-FNA’s utility in DBS diagnosis, particularly when mass lesions are involved, aligning with prior research. During EUS-FNA procedures, practitioners are particularly concerned with the choice of needle type. In DBSs, the 2 most frequently used needle types are 22-gauge and 25-gauge. Tomoda and colleagues’ [ ] study found that for 88 patients with pancreatic lesions, the 25-gauge Franseen needle was as effective as the 22-gauge Franseen needle in tissue acquisition and showed no significant difference in diagnostic performance. This finding aligns with the results of Gimeno-García and colleagues’ study on 120 cases of gastrointestinal and adjacent organ solid lesions. [ ] In terms of diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, our study’s outcomes were consistent with previous research. However, we did not evaluate the quality of the obtained specimens. Consequently, based on these research findings, the 25-gauge needle seems to have a comparative advantage in the selection of needle type. EUS-FNA is a multistep procedure influenced by various uncertain factors, resulting in variability in pathology sampling quality. [ – ] Our study alone observed suboptimal sampling in 6.8% of patients, highlighting a need for improved techniques. One potential solution is ROSE, involving real-time assessment of sample adequacy and diagnostic yield. [ ] However, the debate surrounding the necessity of ROSE persisted for 2 decades. A meta-analysis of 34 studies aimed to determine whether ROSE impacts the diagnostic accuracy of EUS-FNA in solid pancreatic lesions. [ ] The findings revealed that ROSE remained an independent determinant of EUS-FNA accuracy ( P = 0.001). Yet, a systematic review by Kong et al., [ ] encompassing 7 studies with 1299 patients, indicated that EUS-FNA with ROSE did not enhance diagnostic yield or adequacy. Furthermore, attempts to reduce ROSE’s labor costs led some centers to explore whether endoscopists could replace cytologists for evaluation. However, results have been unfavorable. A double-blind prospective controlled trial demonstrated that even well-trained endoscopists were less accurate than cytopathologists in assessing specimen adequacy ( P = 0.004) and providing a preliminary estimate of malignancy ( P < 0.001). [ ] Looking ahead, advancements in deep-learning techniques and increased computational power hold promise for the application of artificial intelligence in enhancing ROSE accuracy while reducing costs. [ ] This avenue may lead to more precise and cost-effective ROSE procedures in the future. EUS plays a pivotal role not only in obtaining pathological tissue for diagnostic purposes but also in using advanced techniques such as EUS elastography (EUS-E) and contrast-enhanced EUS (CE-EUS) to broaden its diagnostic capabilities in the context of DBSs. Both EUS-E and CE-EUS offer qualitative, semiquantitative, and quantitative methods for the differential diagnosis of DBSs. [ ] Although EUS-E and CE-EUS have been extensively studied in the context of pancreatic lesions, with several meta-analyses demonstrating high sensitivity (92%–98%), their specificity in diagnosing malignant pancreatic tumors remains relatively low (67%–76%). [ ] Notably, Kitano et al. [ ] focused on CE-EUS and reported pooled estimates of sensitivity and specificity at 93% (91%–95%) and 80% (75%–85%), respectively, for this clinical application. It is worth highlighting that there is a dearth of reports on the use of EUS-E and CE-EUS specifically for the assessment of bile duct occupancy alone within the existing literature. This underscores the potential for further exploration and research in this important diagnostic area. [ ] focused on CE-EUS and reported pooled estimates of sensitivity and specificity at 93% (91%–95%) and 80% (75%–85%), respectively, for this clinical application. It is worth highlighting that there is a dearth of reports on the use of EUS-E and CE-EUS specifically for the assessment of bile duct occupancy alone within the existing literature. This underscores the potential for further exploration and research in this important diagnostic area. It is important to recognize that the growing awareness of IgG4-RD and the establishment of globally recognized diagnostic criteria have led to an increasing prevalence of bile duct stenosis attributed to IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis. [ ] This entity now represents a significant portion of benign bile duct stenosis cases and warrants careful consideration in the differential diagnosis. In our study, we diagnosed 33 cases of bile duct stenosis attributed to IgG4-RDs, comprising 28% of all benign bile duct stenosis cases. Diagnosing IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis poses a clinical challenge, as it can manifest with markedly elevated tumor marker levels and limited stenosis on imaging when other extrabiliary organs remain unaffected. [ ] This can easily lead to misdiagnosis as a malignant stenosis. A comprehensive diagnostic approach should encompass typical histopathologic, clinical, serologic, and imaging findings when assessing IgG4-RD. Diagnostic criteria for this condition have evolved from organ-specific and general benchmarks in the 20th century to the 2019 ACR/EULAR classification criteria. [ , ] In a multicenter retrospective study of patients with kidney disease, these latest ACR/EULAR criteria demonstrated strong performance (sensitivity 90.9%, specificity 98%, PPV 98%, and NPV 90.7%). [ ] However, further prospective studies are necessary to validate these criteria in clinical practice. Our study had several limitations. First, the study did not uniformly use ROSE during EUS-FNA procedures. ROSE can enhance the assessment of sample adequacy and diagnostic yield. However, its inconsistent use in this study may have impacted the diagnostic accuracy and completeness of results. Second, this study was conducted in a single center, which might introduce selection bias and limit the generalizability of findings. Multicenter studies with diverse patient populations could provide a broader perspective on the diagnostic performance of EUS-FNA. Moreover, although this study identified cases of bile duct stenosis due to IgG4-RDs, diagnosing these conditions can be challenging due to their varied clinical presentations and imaging findings. The criteria used were based on the 2019 ACR/EULAR classification criteria, but further prospective validation studies are needed to confirm their utility. These limitations should be considered when interpreting the results and applying them to clinical practice. In summary, our investigation substantiates the pivotal role of EUS-FNA within the diagnostic framework for DBSs. The robust diagnostic sensitivity and specificity exhibited by EUS-FNA reinforce its significance as an invaluable diagnostic modality in this domain. Our analysis identified that the primary determinants influencing the diagnostic efficacy of EUS-FNA were the presence or absence of a discernible mass shadow surrounding the DBSs and the dimensions of this observed mass shadow. Furthermore, our findings emphasize the relevance of considering IgG4-RDs, which constitute a substantial portion of cases, during the differential diagnosis of these strictures.

chunks.content: Introduction Heel pain is one of the most common reasons for visits to orthopedic clinics and is often associated with plantar fasciopathy . Plantar fasciopathy is a clinical condition that may include calcaneal spur (enthesophyte) formation and is considered an important etiological factor in heel pain , . Although the relationship between calcaneal spurs and symptoms is controversial in the literature, the presence of spurs is often seen in conjunction with thickening of the plantar fascia and is taken into account in clinical evaluations , . Calcaneal spur formation is associated primarily with biomechanical factors . These factors include; advanced age, obesity, long periods of standing, repeated micro-trauma, and decreased ankle dorsiflexion , , . For the evaluation of heel pain using imaging studies the most common study is the lateral view of the foot on plain film. While the primary limitation of this method is that it does not allow direct visualization of findings from plantar fasciitis, it is frequently employed for initial screening purposes. Ultrasonography and MRI are preferred methods when dealing with more chronic or complicated cases, as they provide better resolution for a more thorough assessment of plantar fascia pathology including thickening or edema – . The use of radiographs as an information source for clinical decision support systems has many advantages including; radiographs are relatively inexpensive, readily available, and quickly applied , . However, there may be significant variability in how radiologists interpret radiographs, which can complicate making accurate diagnoses especially when early stage spur formation appears similar to typical heel images . Thus, developing CAD (computer-aided diagnosis) systems that are either completely or partially automated would be of value to clinicians by helping them make informed decisions when using radiology . There has been significant advancement in DL (deep learning) methods used for medical image analysis over the last few years and as a result, they have provided accurate results in both classification and lesion detection , , but these models are dependent upon having access to large amounts of data and high levels of computing capability , to produce successful outcomes. Additionally, it is anticipated that no one DL architecture will provide the best possible outcomes for all types of tasks . With respect to Deep Feature Engineering (DFE), we are now in a position to apply many of the ideas previously discussed. The use of pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for the extraction of deep features combined with the application of the traditional methods of feature selection and classification offers a lighter, more flexible, and more generally applicable alternative to the aforementioned architectures. Because of its ability to produce good results on small datasets, DFE is particularly well-suited to problems such as the detection of calcaneal spurs from routine lateral foot radiographs. A DFE approach based upon the combination of the features produced by 19 different pre-trained CNNs enhanced by INCA-based feature selection and a tkNN classifier is proposed in this paper. The purpose of this DFE approach is to obtain accurate classifications of calcaneal spur presence/absence, to achieve consistent performance regardless of the amount of training data available, and to facilitate clinical decision making. Thus, it aims to increase consistency in conservative treatment planning and to strengthen clinician-patient communication , . Literature review Plantar fasciopathy and calcaneal spur are among the most common causes of heel pain and are clinical conditions that require careful evaluation in both diagnosis and treatment , . In recent years, artificial intelligence and deep learning-based methods have begun to play an important role in medical image analysis and clinical decision support systems . These developments enable more objective, rapid, and reproducible results, particularly in different modalities such as radiography, ultrasound, and pressure sensor-based images , . Taher and Özacar presented HeCapsNet, a capsule network for heel disease detection from lateral foot radiographs. They extended the baseline CapsNet with convolution, dropout and max-pooling layers. Their dataset included 3,956 images. They also utilized YOLOv8 to aid the classification step. Their model obtained a test accuracy of 97.29% on the balanced dataset and 95.77% accuracy under five-fold cross validation. Kim et al. designed a deep learning model for insole prescription based on clinical and biomechanical data of 838 patients with foot pain. The variables that were entered into the model were pelvic obliquity, anterversions and retroversion. Their system forecasted foot posture index and the necessity for supportive components according to modified Root technique. They experimented with two deep neural network regression models, and five multi-class deep neural network classifier models. Their validation accuracy varied from 72% to 95%, and the area under receiver operating characteristic curve was between 0.79 and 0.94. Their models achieved greater than 90% accuracy at both heel lift and full lift decisions. Roop et al. introduced a self-supervised learning approach to estimate the probe angle

with foot pain. The variables that were entered into the model were pelvic obliquity, anterversions and retroversion. Their system forecasted foot posture index and the necessity for supportive components according to modified Root technique. They experimented with two deep neural network regression models, and five multi-class deep neural network classifier models. Their validation accuracy varied from 72% to 95%, and the area under receiver operating characteristic curve was between 0.79 and 0.94. Their models achieved greater than 90% accuracy at both heel lift and full lift decisions. Roop et al. introduced a self-supervised learning approach to estimate the probe angle of plantar fascia ultrasound images. Over 3600 ultrasound frames from thirteen healthy individuals were enrolled in the study. These frames were artificially rotated from negative forty-five to positive forty-five degrees. Their system employed a ResNet-50 encoder pretrained on RadImageNet and a support vector machine regression model to obtain the angle. Their technique achieved average absolute error of 2.98 degrees, and we observed the anticipated monotonic increase in angle on new data collected. Alyanak et al. compared artificial intelligence with human experts in measuring plantar fascia thickness and examined the reliability of ChatGPT-4 measurements on magnetic resonance imaging data. Their dataset included forty-one cases. Human observers showed excellent internal consistency with intraclass correlation values above 0.98. ChatGPT-4 produced low reliability with intraclass correlation values between 0.39 and 0.43 and high error rates with mean relative error reaching 77%, especially in samples with thin plantar fascia. Rajagopal et al. developed an artificial intelligence framework consisting of VGG16-GRU, autoencoder + random forest, and LSTM-ensembled XGBoost models for personalized foot health management. In their study, nine different walking postures were classified using pressure sensor heat maps (98.3% accuracy), automatic diagnosis was performed for 12 different foot diseases (92.7% accuracy), and personalized shoe recommendations were then provided. Personalization of the recommended designs was achieved using Stable Diffusion-based synthetic shoe images, thereby increasing both clinical accuracy and user satisfaction. Yin et al. established an artificial neural network model for forecasting treatment effect among patients with chronic plantar fasciitis receiving the extracorporeal shock wave therapy. A multilayer perceptron with ten input factors that were patient age, sex, body mass index, symptom duration, visual analog scale score, edema and spurs on radiographs was used by the system. They trained the model to an accuracy of 92.50%. Beyond end-to-end deep learning, a growing body of research has explored the integration of pre-trained CNN features with tr aditional machine learning classifiers for biomedical image analysis, particularly when training data is limited. Wang et al. combined deep features extracted from VGG16 and GoogLeNet with an extreme learning machine (ELM) classifier for breast cancer detection and achieved 97.58% accuracy on the BreaKHis dataset. Celik et al. extracted features from ResNet50 and fed them into an SVM classifier for skin lesion classification, reporting improved performance compared to end-to-end fine-tuning on small datasets. Amin et al. proposed a framework for brain tumor classification that used pre-trained CNN features with multiple classical classifiers including SVM, kNN, and random forest, and demonstrated that the SVM-based pipeline achieved the highest accuracy. Nahiduzzaman et al. used hybrid features from EfficientNet and DenseNet concatenated with machine learning classifiers for grading of diabetic retinopathy, and demonstrated that the fusion was superior to deep models on small data. Abdar et al. analysed the utility of transfer learning with traditional classifiers in medical image analysis, and concluded that this hybrid approach is an effective solution to overcome data deficiency in clinical settings. These works demonstrate that integrating deep feature representations from the existing models with traditional classification algorithms can be effective, but they are generally designed based on a single CNN backbone and thus only learn a limited variety of features and classifiers. The limitations of state-of-the-art frameworks promoted us to combine 19 pretrained CNN-based features into an INCA-tkNN-IMV architecture in a flexible DFE setup. Literature gaps Despite the success of end-to-end deep learning in large-scale image classification, its application to small clinical datasets remains constrained by two fundamental limitations. First, deep learning models are data-hungry; these models tend to overfit and do not generalize well in the event of limited training samples , . Second, the training and deployment of deep networks are computationally expensive; thus their practical utilization in resource-constrained clinical settings is limited for complex models . Apart from these common restrictions, a third less examined constraint is the diversity in feature representation. Existing deep learning methods mainly use single CNN backbone for feature representation, which not only limits the diversity between learned features of each class but also makes learned features sensitive to inter-class visual similarity , . Although the above-mentioned recent studies have shown that combining pre-trained CNN descriptors with traditional classifiers can partially solve the small-data problem, these hybrid approaches usually utilize only a single backbone and a single classifier for detection, thus multi-network descriptor fusion as well as ensemble classification has not been investigated in calcaneal spur detection. Motivation and our method Deep learning has made tremendous advances in medical image analysis by hierarchical feature learning from raw data , , and CNNs based on spatially-organized tensor structure have proved to be convincingly trained for tasks in radiology and orthopedic domain . However, regardless of their outstanding performance, the direct utilization of advanced CNNs on certain tasks such as detection of calcaneal spur is not trivial for three fundamental reasons: (1) large quantity of annotated training datasets are required but this is not feasible in specialized clinical domains; (2) requires substantially compute resources to optimize and inference model; and (3) there does exist a single CNN network that works always best for all the imaging tasks . These issues concurrently motivate the investigations of deep-feature engineering (DFE) approaches that combine representation power from several pretrained CNNs and outlay computational expense close to classic feature selection and classification techniques. Feature engineering (FE), an earlier technique that is still effective in terms of processing time for smaller sets of data, however does not have sufficient capacity to model the non-linear complexities of biomedical image analysis , has created a need for the development of deep feature engineering (DFE) methodologies that integrate the high level of representation provided by CNNs with the rapid processing capability of FE. DFE methodologies incorporate three components: Pretrained CNNs for transferable features; Iterative feature selection to improve the quality of the representation; and. Ensemble strategies such as iterative majority voting (IMV) to provide stable results. In this research, 19 CNN Backbones were integrated with INCA feature selection and a tkNN ensemble classification algorithm to both increase accuracy and robustness of the results. The detection of calcaneal spur from X-ray images using the proposed DFE methodology offers a reliable solution for the clinical application to detect calcaneal spurs in limited data sets where the difference between the classes can be subtle. The presented deep feature engineering model The DFE framework aims to deliver accurate classification on limited image data. It combines multiple processing stages to strengthen prediction. The pipeline includes five phases: (i) feature extraction with 19 pretrained CNNs, (ii) feature selection through INCA , (iii) classification by a tkNN ensemble, (iv) generation of fused outputs by IMV , and (v) final choice of the top result using a greedy algorithm . Deep features are first taken from the global average pooling or fully connected layer of each CNN, giving 19 feature vectors. Then, INCA keeps only the most relevant features in each vector. Thus, tkNN ensemble provides classification outputs on different settings. IMV combines these outputs to capture complementary strengths across the networks. Then a greedy step picks the configuration with the best accuracy. Figure depicts the workflow in the form of Turker Sengul Machine (TSM). Formally defined as a state machine, the TSM characterizes structure of the recommended model by mapping transitions over feature extraction, selection, classification and fusion to the final decision. TSM adds reproducibility. Readers are able to reconstruct the workflow based on the state diagram without relying exclusively on narrative text. This also permits inter-model comparisons, since different pipelines can themselves be expressed in this same state machine framework. TSM also bridges the gap between algorithms and systems engineering. The model can be built, tested and scaled systematically because the DFE is specified as a state machine. This ensures the building of future pipelines in which states or transitions may replace or augment previous ones. The proposed DFE model consists of the following steps: Step 1 Resize the input medical images into different dimensions such as 224 × 224, 227 × 227, 256 × 256, and 299 × 299 for compatibility with different CNNs. Step 2 Extract deep features from the last GAP/FC7 layer of 19 pretrained CNNs (SqueezeNet , MobileNetV2 , ResNet50 , DarkNet53 , AlexNet , ShuffleNet , DenseNet201 , InceptionV3 , InceptionResNetV2 , VGG16 , VGG19 , ResNet18 , ResNet101 , DarkNet19 , EfficientNetB0 , NASNetMobile , NASNetLarge , Xception , GoogLeNet . This step extracts 19 feature vectors using these 19 pretrained CNNs. Step 3 : Apply INCA to select the most informative features. Iterations run from 50 to 500, producing 451 subsets. A kNN classifier (k = 1, L1 distance, equal weights, 10-fold CV) evaluates each subset. In this research, the start and stop values of the iteration is chosen 50 and 500 respectively. In this respect, INCA evaluates 451 (= 500 − 50 + 1) subsets. In this method, kNN classifier (k:1, distance: L1-norm, distance weight: equal, validation: 10-fold CV) has been utilized to compute classification accuracies of the 451 selected features. Table lists the original and selected feature dimensions. Step 4 : Classify the selected features with tkNN classifier using 10-fold CV. Apply multiple parameter settings such as distance metrics, distance weights, and neighbor numbers to generate classifier outcomes. Then, tkNN uses IMV to produce the voted outcomes and by applying greedy algorithm, the final outcome is selected among classifier-wise and voted outcomes. The utilized parameters of tkNN are: Distance metrics Four metrics are evaluated, including cityblock (Manhattan), euclidean, cosine, and spearman. Among the 42 false-positive cases, several images showed subtle calcaneal tuberosity irregularities that may mimic early spur formation. These included mild enthesophytic change at the inferior fascial insertion, slight periosteal irregularity along the distal calcaneal surface, and small focal calcifications near the plantar fascial origin. In addition, some misclassified images showed non-anatomical variability in radiograph quality and mild rotational malpositioning, which may have produced overlapping artifacts resembling spur-like projections. The morphological similarity between normal calcaneal variants and early-stage spurs is a known diagnostic challenge in musculoskeletal radiology. These findings show early enthesophytic changes at the inferior fascial insertion, mild periosteal roughening along the distal surface of the calcaneus, and small focal calcifications near the site of origin. Such features are frequently encountered in clinical practice and can introduce variability between observers even among expert radiologists. In addition, a subset of misclassified lesions displayed non-anatomical diversity in the radiograph quality and we also observed slight rotational malpositioning of the lateral view which could create additional overlapping artefacts within the calcaneal contour that might resemble a spur-like projections. The morphologic similarities between normal variant calcaneal tuberosities and early/first stages of spurs is a well-appreciated diagnostic dilemma in musculoskeletal radiology. These results suggest that the false positives are clustered near the clinical ambiguity, rather than being a function of a systematic bias in the model, and highlight that binary classification in cases where pathology lies on a continuous spectrum is inherently challenging. The model achieved 93.42% accuracy, which demonstrates reliable predictive ability. Also, all results are over 92%. For the no-finding class, sensitivity reached 86.71% and precision reached 96.82%. For the spur class, sensitivity was 98.04% and precision was 91.46%. Specificity values were 98.04% for no-finding and 86.71% for spur, producing a balanced accuracy of 92.37%. These results show that spur cases are detected with high sensitivity, while normal cases are identified with strong precision. The F1-scores were 91.49% and 94.64%. These values suggest that the framework maintains balance between sensitivity and precision on the two classes. A geometric mean of 92.20% shows relatively stable performance when it comes to classification. The lightweight DFE framework overall performs well in identifying calcaneal spur from X-ray images. These results highlight that early fusion, sequential feature selection, and ensemble strategies improve robustness, even on small datasets. Explainability analysis To confirm that the latent attention of the proposed framework is targeted towards clinically relevant macro-anatomic regions instead of background noise, Grad-CAM visualizations were generated with the best CNN backbones. Grad-CAM generates class discriminative heatmaps by taking the gradient of the predicted score with respect to activations from the last convolutional layer, indicating where positive contributions to classification are coming from spatially. Figure includes Grad-CAM heatmaps that identically categorized the calcaneal spur and no finding cases using ResNet50. In spur cases, activation maps are localized to the inferior aspect of the calcaneus, where spurs develop at the plantar calcaneal tuberosity. In the no-finding studies, the heatmap shows widespread activation in calcaneal region without focal concentration on plantar surface. These visualizations also confirm that the pretrained CNNs do learn to attend, in the anatomically expected region for spur detection. The localized activation patterns are consistent with the clinical definition of calcaneal spur and suggest that deep features extracted encode valuable structural information rather than incidental aspects from the image (e.g., background intensity variation, radiograph borders). Besides, the framework runs exclusively under CPU mode with no use of GPU; each CNN does merely a single pass for features extraction with backpropagation or fine-tuning. It is also important to note that calcaneal spur detection is not a time-critical emergency task. In clinical practice, lateral foot radiographs are evaluated as part of routine orthopedic consultations, and a processing time of seconds to minutes is clinically acceptable for a computer-aided decision support tool. Comparison with traditional classifiers To further validate the effectiveness of the proposed DFE framework, comparative experiments were conducted using the same INCA-selected features with several widely used traditional machine learning classifiers. Specifically, the features selected by INCA from the best-performing CNN backbone (ResNet50) were classified using support vector machine (SVM) with radial basis function (RBF) kernel, random forest (RF) with 100 trees, decision tree (DT), logistic regression (LR), and classical kNN (k = 1, cityblock distance, equal weights). All classifiers were evaluated under the same stratified 10-fold cross-validation protocol to ensure a fair comparison. The classification results are presented in Table . These results are shown in Table and show that the proposed tkNN + IMV framework significantly outperforms all of the compared traditional classifiers over all evaluation metrics. Second was SVM (RBF) with 90.84% accuracy, and next came random forest with 89.68%. The decision tree classifier achieved the worst classification performance (83.87%) since it could not capture complex feature interactions well. The lack of performance in classical kNN at 85.03% and the superior accuracy of our proposed tkNN compared to it with 93.42%, underlines the efficacy of multi-parameter exploration, iterative majority voting over candidate set and greedy selection among them while forming an ensemble in tkNN component. Although SVM and random forest are powerful classifiers included in this work which can gain from the INCA features, they do not have tkNN’s fusion scheme to merge the complementary classification results from various parameter settings. These results justifiy that the DFE framework benefits not only from the expressiveness capacity of deep CNN features but also from its structured ensemble and fusion strategy to achieve better classification performance, which can hardly be mimicked by replacing the classifier component with a conventional one. An ablation study was performed following the same stratified 10-fold cross-validation protocol to analyze the contribution of each module in the proposed framework. There was initially a base case, and the elements were then progressively introduced in order to calculate their additional impact. The results are reported in Table . The ablation results reveal the incremental contribution of each module. Replacing INCA with standard NCA (C1 vs. C2) reduced accuracy by approximately 2.58% points, confirming that the iterative subset evaluation strategy of INCA yields a more discriminative feature set than single-shot NCA selection. The transition from classical kNN to tkNN (C2 vs. C3) produced the largest improvement of approximately 7.10% points, demonstrating that the multi-parameter ensemble mechanism of tkNN is the most influential component in the framework. The addition of IMV with greedy selection (C3 vs. C4) further improved accuracy by 1.29% points, validating that information fusion across multiple CNN outcomes captures complementary representations that no single backbone can provide. These results confirm that each module contributes independently to the overall performance. Test of additional dataset To demonstrate the general classification ability of the proposed DFE model, a publicly available dataset named SIPaKMeD was used . The SIPaKMeD dataset contains five classes: Dyskeratotic: 813 cell images. Koilocytotic: 825 cell images. Metaplastic: 793 cell images. Parabasal: 787 cell

The addition of IMV with greedy selection (C3 vs. C4) further improved accuracy by 1.29% points, validating that information fusion across multiple CNN outcomes captures complementary representations that no single backbone can provide. These results confirm that each module contributes independently to the overall performance. Test of additional dataset To demonstrate the general classification ability of the proposed DFE model, a publicly available dataset named SIPaKMeD was used . The SIPaKMeD dataset contains five classes: Dyskeratotic: 813 cell images. Koilocytotic: 825 cell images. Metaplastic: 793 cell images. Parabasal: 787 cell images. Superficial-intermediate: 831 cell images. The model was applied to this dataset, and the classification outcomes are presented in Fig. . Figure presents the classification results of our proposed DFE model on SIPaKMeD dataset. The tkNN based accuracies of 19 CNN features sets are presented in Figure (a). Performance varied across networks. DenseNet201 produced the maximum accuracy (96.86%) and SqueezeNet resulted in the lowest value (81.08%). On average the accuracy of all CNN models was 91.73% (SD = 3.81). The models with the best accuracy were those of ResNet50, DarkNet53, and EfficientNetB0, which were all higher than 94%. This suggests that they leverage deeper and more efficient networks, which can capture stronger representations in contrast to old or light models achieving weaker ones. In Fig. (b) we show results of the extended majority voting. Seventeen voting results were assessed, between 96.37 and 97.43%. The highest voted result is 97.43%, which is 0.57% point higher than the best single CNN accuracy. The stability of the ensemble fusion is further validated by its standard deviation (0.34%). These results highlight two conclusions. First, individual CNNs show different classification abilities, which underlines the importance of using diverse models. Second, IMV improves accuracy and stability, since all voted outcomes surpassed most single CNNs. The DFE framework therefore integrates complementary features successfully and achieves reliable performance on a challenging cytology dataset. The best classification results were obtained with DenseNet201, ResNet50, and ResNet101. The remaining 16 CNN models were not required to achieve 97.43% accuracy on this dataset. The corresponding confusion matrix is displayed in Fig. . From this confusion matrix, accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score were calculated. These results are summarized in Table . All classification metrics exceeded 97.4%. These classification results demonstrate that the presented DFE model attained high classification performance on the five-classes cell image dataset. This dataset has five classes and to evaluate class-wise classification performance, we have demonstrated precision-recall (P-R) curve in Fig. . Figure illustrated precision and recall across the five SIPaKMeD categories. Recall spans 91.76–99.52%, while precision falls between 95.16 and 99.11%. The Koilocytotic group (Class 2) showcases the lowest recall (91.76%) but preserves strong precision (98.18%). Dyskeratotic (Class 1), Parabasal (Class 4), and Superficial-intermediate (Class 5) achieve recall above 99%. reflecting the reliable detection capacity of the proposed DFE model. Mean precision equals 97.46% (Standard Deviation – SD – 1.76%), and mean recall equals 97.45% (SD 3.32%). Mean F1-score is 97.42%, with class values between 94.86% and 99.30%. Logit-based 95% CIs are 94.87–99.18% for precision and 93.77–99.72% for recall. These intervals stay within the 0–100% range and confirm consistency. A paired t-test shows no significant gap between precision and recall ( p ≈ 0.997), which highlights balanced sensitivity and specificity. The comparative results for the SIPaKMeD dataset are reported in Table . The proposed TSM-based DFE approach in this study demonstrates competitive and high performance when compared to current methods in the literature. In particular, the 97.43% accuracy achieved with 10-fold cross-validation outperforms the CBAM + parallel CNN approach (92.82%) proposed by Comert et al. , the data augmentation ResNet50V2 + Self-Attention approach reported in the study by Wubineh et al. (5 classes: 92%), and the specialized CNN-based model proposed by Alsubai et al. (91.13%). Furthermore, similar accuracy levels have been achieved with the deep feature fusion-based approach proposed by Fang et al. (96.02%) and the data augmentation-based ensemble model in the study by Sahoo et al. (97.18%). When compared to the MSENet-based model developed by Pramanik et al. (97.21%), our proposed method achieves higher accuracy, demonstrating the effectiveness of the INCA + tkNN + IMV integration in enhancing generalizability, particularly on small datasets. Furthermore, when compared to the Transformer-based CerviFormer model (93.70%) proposed by Deo et al. , the fact that the proposed method achieves higher success despite using a hybrid feature engineering approach instead of classical deep networks indicates that the method can produce more stable results in cases of data diversity and imbalance. These values surpass or match prior SIPaKMeD benchmarks (95–97%), placing the DFE pipeline among the leading models for cytology analysis. Stability across classes, coupled with limited false positives, strengthens its case for integration into clinical screening workflows. Findings and advantages The findings, advantages,

These values surpass or match prior SIPaKMeD benchmarks (95–97%), placing the DFE pipeline among the leading models for cytology analysis. Stability across classes, coupled with limited false positives, strengthens its case for integration into clinical screening workflows. Findings and advantages The findings, advantages, limitations and future works of this research are discussed as below. Findings : The proposed framework achieved a classification accuracy of 93.42% on the curated calcaneal spur X-ray dataset. Sensitivity values were 86.71% for the no-finding class and 98.04% for the spur class, while specificity values were 98.04% and 86.71%, respectively. Precision reached 96.82% for no finding and 91.46% for spur, and the F1-scores were 91.49% and 94.64%. The geometric mean was calculated as 92.20%. These results highlight that the model maintained consistent performance across both classes. IMV produced 17 voted outcomes. The highest accuracy was 93.42%, which is 1.29% points higher than the best tkNN outcome (92.13%). Vote 5 was selected as the final model. It was generated from seven CNNs: DarkNet53, DenseNet201, ResNet50, EfficientNetB0, ResNet101, ShuffleNet, and InceptionV3. These CNNs are enough to obtain the best classification performance. The per-CNN analysis showcased that individual accuracies ranged between 84.00% (SqueezeNet) and 92.13% (ResNet50 and DenseNet201), with an average accuracy of 89.04%. The confusion matrix reported 274 correct no-finding cases, 450 correct spur cases, 42 false positives, and 9 false negatives. Errors were concentrated in the no-finding class. This outcome reflects both the visual similarity between normal heel structures and early spur formations, and the imbalanced distribution of the dataset. Advantages : The proposed framework is lightweight and does not require GPU acceleration. This property ensures practical use in clinical environments with limited computational resources. 19 pretrained CNNs are combined through feature extraction and fusion. This approach leverages the complementary strengths of different architectures and avoids the weaknesses of single backbones. INCA is applied to retain the most informative features. This process reduces redundancy and improves the discriminative power of the features. The use of tkNN with IMV increases classification stability. Multiple outcomes are evaluated and the best-performing one is selected through a greedy strategy. The TSM is adopted to represent the workflow as a state machine. This design improves clarity, and reproducibility of the model. Each phase of the framework, including feature extraction, selection, classification, voting, and greedy optimization, is transparent. This structure provides interpretability and allows independent analysis of each stage. Limitations and future works Limitation : The exploratory phase of the framework utilizes 19 pretrained CNNs, which increases the total feature extraction time during model development. However, the deployment configuration requires only seven CNNs, as identified by the IMV and greedy selection stages, which substantially reduces the inference cost. Future work will focus on optimizing the inference pipeline through GPU-based parallel feature extraction and model pruning strategies to further minimize processing time. The dataset used in this study is limited in size and focused only on calcaneal spur detection. Broader validation with larger and more diverse datasets is necessary to test robustness. Future directions : The framework will also be evaluated on larger X-ray databases which cover additional musculoskeletal diseases. Determining the generalizability of this approach was the objective in this extension. The computational burden of feature extraction and selection will be minimized to cut implementation time and resource needs. Hybrid integration with other machine learning classifiers will be studied to achieve better classification accuracy and computational scalability. The DFE method will be developed for real-time clinical settings where rapid and accurate diagnosis is needed. Potential applications : The suggested model can be applied in the diagnosis of orthopedics to manually assist the radiologists for identification of calcaneal spurs from X-ray images. Part of hospital information system as a reliable classification result decision supporting tool. The lightweight structure of the framework allows its use in clinical environments with limited computational resources. It can be adapted to other small biomedical image datasets such as rare musculoskeletal disorders where large-scale deep learning models are less effective. By using the TSM and the structured classification pipeline, a physical AI model can be recommended. The introduced DFE framework has potential in telemedicine applications through remote analysis of X-ray images in underserved regions. It can also support personalized treatment planning by identifying subtle variations in heel structures and assisting patient-specific evaluations. Conclusions This study presented a new deep feature engineering framework for calcaneal spur detection in X-ray images. The framework used 19 pretrained CNNs for feature extraction, iterative feature selection with INCA,

small biomedical image datasets such as rare musculoskeletal disorders where large-scale deep learning models are less effective. By using the TSM and the structured classification pipeline, a physical AI model can be recommended. The introduced DFE framework has potential in telemedicine applications through remote analysis of X-ray images in underserved regions. It can also support personalized treatment planning by identifying subtle variations in heel structures and assisting patient-specific evaluations. Conclusions This study presented a new deep feature engineering framework for calcaneal spur detection in X-ray images. The framework used 19 pretrained CNNs for feature extraction, iterative feature selection with INCA, classification with tkNN, outcome fusion with IMV (it is an information fusion function), and final selection with a greedy algorithm. The model reached 93.42% accuracy on the curated dataset and performed well on a difficult medical imaging problem. Spur cases were detected with high sensitivity, while no-finding cases were harder to classify because normal heel images can resemble early spur cases. Precision and F1-scores showed that false predictions were limited. IMV produced 17 voted outcomes and improved accuracy compared with single CNN or tkNN outcomes. The results also showed that the best performance was obtained with only seven CNNs, which reduced computational cost while keeping accuracy high. The proposed framework is lightweight, efficient, and suitable for other biomedical image analysis tasks where datasets are small and accurate decisions are needed.
